A record the target cannot represent is converted exactly where an exact form exists (a polyline becomes a degree-1 B-spline; an elliptic cone becomes a rational NURBS surface), or dropped or degraded with a loss naming its id. A writer never stores application-private data in a target file to be read back; every fact is written in the target format's own state. A partial face is not written by a writer of another codec, with `export:face.partial` naming it. A region that is marked, or that holds a marked shell or a partial face, is written as shells and never as a solid, with `export:solid.partial` naming it. Each shell is closed or open as the faces written for it make it: a void not stated leaves an exterior that was read whole a closed shell, and a face not written leaves its shell open. The target's form is the one it has for a shell that bounds no stated volume: a STEP `SHELL_BASED_SURFACE_MODEL` of closed or open shells; an IGES shell in no manifold solid; a sheet body only where the written shell is open; and, in a target where faces joined into a closed shell are a solid (Rhino), the faces unjoined. A target with no such form omits the region with the same loss. A marked body's other regions are written as they are. A face on an `Unknown` surface is written as the carrier allows, under this section's rule for it.

**Lowering a typed operation.** A writer writes each typed operation in the first of these forms its target admits:
1. The target's equivalent primitive.
2. Where the target has none, an equivalent construction from the target's own features that has the same meaning under every edit of its inputs: a triangular-section coil as a helix and a sweep of a triangle sketch, a wedge primitive as a ruled loft between its two rectangles. The writer emits definitions and the target application evaluates them, so no kernel is needed. The construction keeps every parameter binding the target can express. The report charges `export:feature.lowered` (Info) naming the feature and the construction used. A construction is admissible only where the writer can follow these rules without a kernel; where it cannot, step 3 applies:
   - **States.** A construction's geometry features are those that are not stateless (§5.4). The last of them takes the source feature's state, and every earlier one has no stored state. A target that takes feature definitions over the current geometry (SolidWorks, NX, Creo, CATIA) writes them as it writes every feature (States, below). A full-shape target (FreeCAD) writes each earlier one without a shape and marks it for recompute (FreeCAD `Touched`). A target that holds no feature without its state (Fusion) cannot take a construction with more than one geometry feature, and step 3 applies.
   - **Picks inside a construction.** A later feature of a construction may pick the whole result of an earlier one, its body or its curve, which a reference to that feature states. A pick of an earlier one's faces, edges, or vertices is admissible only where the writer can state it from a state the document holds, by name; an entity that exists only between two of the construction's features is in no state the document holds, and step 3 applies.
   - **Names downstream.** The writer maps each name the source gives the lowered feature's entities to the construction's entity where a naming rule established for the target covers the construction's features (Names, below). Where none does, each later pick of those entities is written in the target's unresolved-reference form, and the loss is charged on that pick at Warning, naming the picking feature and the lowered one. `export:feature.lowered` stays Info and names the construction.
   - **Outputs a writer creates.** A construction that needs a definition the document does not have is an output the writer creates: `plan` lists it, keyed by the occurrence it serves, and the caller names it like any other output, an unnamed one being refused before anything is written (Encode sets, above). An occurrence's own parameter values (§5.1) are written, in this order, as a configuration of the prototype that the occurrence selects, with those values as its parameter overrides, where the target has configurations; else as a copy of the prototype's definition with those values, which the occurrence places in its stead, an output the writer creates where definitions are files, and which no longer follows an edit of the prototype, a loss naming the occurrence.
3. Where no construction exists, the feature's result as stored geometry at its position, where the document holds that state, with a loss naming the feature.
4. Otherwise the feature is dropped with a loss naming it.

A writer stores no application-private data in the target to mark a lowered construction, and a decoder recognises none: a decode of the written file states the construction's own features. A `Native` operation and a `native_options` entry, filed under the same cases (Rule N case (a), or a typed fact whose carrier is unread; among them a parameter's tolerance keys, §5.12, and a PMI annotation's native values, §8), are written only by a writer of their codec (W1, W2); every other writer charges a loss naming the record that holds them. A `source_settings` entry (case (b)) is written only by a writer of its codec; every other writer ignores it and charges nothing. A record that carries `native_options` and `source_settings` (an operation, a sketch and its entities and constraints, a datum, a sheet-metal rule, a construction's mode, a parameter (§5.12), and a PMI annotation (§8); a `Transition` carries `native_options` only) keeps its native values in them by case. A `SourceAttribute` (§8) holds only a user-visible property, which every writer writes; a decoder never states a record's native value as a `SourceAttribute`.

**Occurrence placements.** A design writer writes an occurrence's placement as the target stores placements. Where the target stores a matrix, it writes the map. Where the target stores a positive uniform scale beside normalized axes (a STEP mapped item, an IGES Type 408 instance), it writes that scale when the linear part is a positive scalar times an orthogonal matrix, the scalar equal to that factor within the relative tolerance of a dimensionless cache (part 10), and writes the normalized axes as the placement; a reflection is the axes' sense, not a negative scale. Where the target stores per-axis factors beside a proper rigid placement (FreeCAD), it writes `Place.scale` as stored, a negative factor included, and writes `placement` as the rigid factor; it does not derive those factors by a polar decomposition. Where the target places components rigidly (SolidWorks, Inventor, Creo, NX, CATIA), it uses an exact form the target has: a uniform positive scale as a scaled derived part (Inventor `ScaleForDerivedMember`), a reflection as a linked mirror part where the target has one. Otherwise, with `A = R·S` the polar decomposition of the map's linear part (`R` orthogonal, `S` symmetric positive definite), it writes the occurrence at the proper rotation `R·F` and the map's translation, as an occurrence of a definition of its own that holds the prototype's bodies under `F·S`; `F` is the identity where `det R` is 1, and otherwise the reflection the target's mirrored part applies, or the reflection in the prototype's XY plane where the target has none. That definition is an output the writer creates (Lowering, outputs a writer creates). The writer charges a loss naming the occurrence where the copy does not follow an edit of the prototype.

**Residual bytes.** For byte positions no decoder reads, the writer uses the value the format specification states. When the specification states none, the writer charges `export:record.residual-unavailable` naming the record.

**States.** A writer to a format that stores per-feature states writes each state the document holds that it can encode in the format's state encoding, at its position. Full-shape formats take any state (FreeCAD per-object shapes). A delta-chain writer encodes a state only where it can produce a chain its target accepts: an F3D writer writes ASM history states; a SolidWorks or NX writer writes the current partition, because a Parasolid delta chain built from neutral states is not established as acceptable. A body that a later feature consumes stays in the format's stored model with the format's hidden marking where the format keeps consumed bodies (F3D).

**Features without their state.** A feature whose state the target needs and the document lacks, or whose state or input names the writer cannot produce for the target, charges `export:evaluation.missing` naming the feature. The writer never substitutes another position's state and never encodes a missing state with a value the format uses for another fact. Where the target's state encoding chains each state to its predecessor (an F3D ASM history), such a feature ends the stated run: the features after it in its container are written as if their states were absent, whether or not the document holds them. A full-shape target (FreeCAD) receives every state the document holds, at its position, and loses only the features whose states are missing. The current state at an unstated rollback (§5.2) is no member's state: a writer never takes it for the state after the container's last member, so a feature whose state would come from it alone is a feature without its state.

A target that takes feature definitions over the current geometry (FreeCAD, SolidWorks, NX, Creo, CATIA) writes each feature's definition, with every state it can encode, and the application rebuilds the features when the user asks; the written history's final state is the current geometry, shown exactly once. Where an ordered container's `rollback` is unstated (§5.2), the writer writes the target's own default for it, the container built through its last member, and that member, where no evaluation states its state, is a feature written without its state (below): the current geometry shown after it is not established as its result. It writes this one form whatever `missing_states` says. A target that holds no feature without its state (Fusion, whose timeline features before the marker each carry a stored state) has two forms, and the caller chooses one (`missing_states`, §3.5):
- **Geometry-true** (the default). The current geometry is written exactly. A timeline is written with its history only where every feature in it can be written with its state and its names. Otherwise the writer writes the parameters and one stored-geometry feature of the current bodies, and charges `export:evaluation.missing` for each feature it does not write. It writes the source's sketches as timeline items before that feature, each on an origin plane or on construction geometry written before it, never on its faces: a Base Feature is a timeline item like any other, and Fusion itself lists sketches and parametric features before one, in regeneration order. A state the writer stores for a feature must be that feature's result: Fusion stores nothing that ties a state to its definition and shows a stored state as stored until something recomputes it, and it has no stale mark (below), so a feature whose exact state the writer cannot produce is a feature without its state.
- **History-true.** The stated run is written with its states, up to the timeline marker, which the writer places after the run's last feature. The later features follow the marker rolled back, with their definitions and without their states (Fusion stores rolled-back features this way), and the final geometry is not shown. The report charges `export:evaluation.missing` naming each rolled-back feature.

A target with no form for a feature at all receives the current geometry as a stored-geometry feature.

Every evaluation whose status is `Stale` or `Failed`, and every feature written without its state, receives the target's stale mark where the format has one (FreeCAD `Touched`, SolidWorks `swConfigurationNeedsUpdate`); otherwise the writer charges `export:evaluation.stale` naming the features. Fusion stores no stale or failure mark.

**Toolpaths.** A writer whose target stores toolpaths writes each toolpath the document holds that it can encode, with the target's stale mark where its status is `Stale` or `Failed` (Fusion `valid="false"`). An operation with no toolpath the writer can encode is written as the target writes an operation not yet generated: in Fusion, with no toolpath file and `valid="false"`, the form Fusion saves itself. A writer never computes a toolpath.

**Names.** A writer stamps each entity it writes with the entity's name in the target's naming scheme. For the same codec it stamps the native name unchanged. For another codec it derives the target's name from the structured name's meaning (feature, role, generator, wrappers) and the target's own allocation rules, finding each entity by its geometry in the state. It derives a name only by a rule established for the target (SolidWorks extrude, cut, revolve, pattern, and mirror faces; Inventor sweep roles; Creo extrude roles; Fusion caps; Fusion side faces of single-loop profiles and hole faces, SolidWorks shell faces and body copies, and CATIA pad and pocket side faces and up-to ends, below). CATIA's rules are read from the procedural report that names each stored face (§5.7). A record of CATIA's compact form, whose definition carries no class selector, names its class by one byte, the catalog entry plus 0x33, and its payload segments by tags of the same offset, so the report's headers that root at such records resolve to features of a named class. Which of the faces these records name a writer can name by the rules below is not established. A pad's or pocket's side face is named by the feature, the key `0`, and the profile element it is swept from. A pad or pocket that ends on a face it finds along its direction (limit codes 4 and 7, §6) makes no end face of its own and names its end by that face. The keys `1` and `2` are no rule for start and end caps, so a writer to CATIA names no cap. Fusion numbers the side faces of a profile by a walk of its loop: take the loop curve with the largest persistent id and the point where it starts as drawn, walk the loop in its stored direction from the curve that leaves that point, and, where the extrusion runs against the profile normal, keep that first curve and reverse the order of the rest; the k-th curve of the walk generates side token k + 2. The rule covers one-sided extrudes and base flanges whose profile is one closed loop of whole lines and arcs. A writer allocates the sketch's curve ids, so it gives the largest id to the loop's newest curve and names every side face of such a profile. It names no side face of a loop with inner loops, a trimmed piece, a circle or spline, the second side of a two-sided or symmetric extrude, or a revolve, whose order is not established (part 11). Fusion names a hole's faces by role, `(1, 3)` the bore wall, `(1, 5)` or `(1, 6)` the flat or drill-point bottom (a decoder reads `(1, 4)` and `(1, 2)` as the flat bottom too), `(1, 7)` and `(1, 8)` a counterbore's wall and floor, and `(2, 10)` a countersink's cone (§5.7), so a writer names the faces of holes of those forms. Fusion attributes a face to the feature that made it, and to a pattern instance, by the references of its name group, read through the document's persistent-id table (type `5D89B935`) in its forward form, which lists each scope's ids: a face whose first reference is one of an `Extrude` scope's ids is that extrude's, a cap where its token is 1 or 2 and a side wall where it is 3 or above, one token per profile curve; and the face named `(s, t, [r…, P, I])`, where `P` and `I` are ids the pattern scope owns, is the instance of the seed face `(s, t, [r…])` that the pattern places, a mirror's image being named the same way. A later feature that modifies a face appends its own id as a negative reference and keeps the rest (`[-372]` becomes `[-372, -396]` under a delete face). A decoder fills a face's `Generated` feature and pattern wrapper by these rules. Which instance coordinate each of a pattern's ids names is read from the instance's geometry, not from a rule, so a writer to Fusion names no pattern-instance face. SolidWorks names each inner face a shell makes by the name of the face it offsets, with no ordinal, and each face of copy k of a Move/Copy Body by the copying feature, k, and the copied face's name, so a writer names those faces from their source faces' names; which edge takes which fillet ordinal is not established (§5.7). An Inventor edge pick is a selector whose generator array a writer can compute from the pick's `Bounded` name (§5.7), but its secondary array is not established, and its key must name a matched attribute stamped on the edge in a stored history state, so a writer to Inventor writes an edge pick in the unresolved-reference form (part 11). An entity with no established target name (no rule exists, or its name has no transferable meaning) takes the form each target states for it, and a pick may use that form only where the target says so:
- **Fusion** gives an imported or Base Feature face `(1, n, [-b])`, the ordinal `n` among the faces of Base Feature `b`. That form states that a Base Feature made the face, and a face with no name group cannot be the operand of a recipe, so Fusion has no form for a face that a feature made. A writer uses `(1, n, [-b])` only on the faces of a stored-geometry feature it writes, and picks them by it. A feature that needs another entity with no established name, in its picks or its results, is a feature whose names the writer cannot produce (Features without their state).
- **FreeCAD.** A writer from another codec writes no element map and no `shadow`, so every entity takes FreeCAD's unnamed form, and a pick is an index into the input shape the writer writes, which FreeCAD rebinds by geometry on recompute (Picks, below).
- **SolidWorks.** The form for a face that no established rule names is not established (§11). A writer writes a pick of such a face in the unresolved-reference form, which SolidWorks reports for repair when the user rebuilds, and charges a loss naming the feature and the pick.
- **Inventor, CATIA, Creo, NX.** Inventor tags imported faces with the opaque `INV_NMX_IMPORT_TAG`, which names no entity a pick can resolve; no form for an unnamed entity is established for any of the four. A writer writes a pick of such an entity in the target's geometric form where it has one, else in its unresolved-reference form (Picks).

A writer never fabricates a role.

**Picks.** A writer finds the entities a pick means by the pick's `resolved` entities where they are present and valid (§5.8), else by the matching rule of §5.7 in the anchored state, else by its witness. Where it stamped those entities' target names, it writes the pick by them. Otherwise it writes the pick in the target's geometric form, with its witness, where the target has one. A geometric form that the target resolves against stored geometry (a FreeCAD index into the input shape, which FreeCAD rebinds by geometry when no element map is written) is written only when the writer writes that geometry. Where the writer can write neither form, it writes the pick in the target's unresolved-reference form, so that the target reports the broken reference, and charges a loss naming the feature and the pick. A writer never writes an index into a null shape.

**Dependency cycles.** A writer to a format that cannot hold a dependency cycle drops one edge of each cycle and charges `export:dependency.cycle-broken` naming the features.

**Refusals.** A writer refuses only where it can write no file the caller asked for, or where the caller's `strictness` refuses what it wrote; a judgement of what the output holds, a path the writer lacks where another writes the file among them, is a report entry. Every writer refusal is one of five `EncodeError` variants. No variant holds free text; there is no `From<CodecError>`.

| Variant | Applies when |
|---|---|
| `UnsupportedTarget(TargetRefusal)` | the requested target names no catalog entry, the catalog has no default, or the writer holds no source bytes of its format and has no synthesis path; its `TargetRefusal` names which |
| `OutputUnnamed { definition: ProductDefinitionId }` | an output the writer will produce has no name in `EncodeInput.outputs` (Encode sets, above); refused before anything is written |
| `ResourceLimit(ResourceLimit)` | a session ceiling of the caller's `ResourceLimits` runs out |
| `Io(std::io::Error)` | a write or seek on the destination fails; constructed only by `?` |
| `StrictRejected(StrictWriteRejection)` | the completed export report holds an entry that `EncodeInput.strictness` refuses; its `StrictWriteRejection { report: Box<ExportReport>, entry: usize }` holds that report and the first such entry, and nothing is written |

A request that names no target inherits where the output file's source is the target's own format, and otherwise takes the catalog default without a loss. A CADIR writer writes each value in its canonical form, the orders of §2.5 included, and a record nested past a bound of §2.5 is a record the target cannot hold (§2.5). A record that a writer drops, or that the document's `scope` leaves out of a CADIR output, takes its annotations with it (§3.2). The CADIR empty file holds no record and states the document-level fields of its input: `fragment`, `scope`, `source`, `tolerances`, and `repro`, whose `roots` and `manifest` are empty and which states no `incomplete_reason`, because each describes records of the file. A field the writer writes that holds a non-finite number, or a value wider than its declared width in the writer's `CAPACITY_FIELDS`, is a value the target cannot hold. The writer degrades the value where it has a degraded form: a text cut at a character boundary to the field's width, with the length or count the format stores beside it rewritten to the cut. Otherwise it drops the record that holds the value, and each record that needs it, as §3.3 drops a record that needs a dropped record; a count the file cannot address drops the entities past it and writes the count it can. Where the value belongs to no record (a document tolerance, a field of the file's header), the writer writes the target's default for an unstated value (§2.4). Each charges `export:value.unwritable` naming the record or the field, and the finding (`cadmpeg_ir::validate` constructs a non-finite finding) or the width. A record the target cannot represent for another reason, a structural precondition of the writer among them, is converted, degraded, or dropped under Content the target cannot hold, with that section's loss. A record that a file needs is dropped with the records that need it and never refused for: an output from which every record was dropped is the target's empty file, with `export:output.empty`. Every other Error that validation finds in what the output writes, of `validate_neutral` or of the target codec's own validation, is written from the canonical side, with `export:record.invalid` naming the record, or the rule where the finding names no record. A check of a value the writer computed itself holds by construction or is a `debug_assert!` naming the invariant. A patch that cannot write an edit takes the next path (Paths). A catalog row the request names that the writer cannot reach from this document, where it can reach another, is written as a row it reaches, with `target.request-displaced` naming both. An `Inherit` target resolves per output file, from that file's source (`Storage::File.source`, else `CadIr.source` for the root's output); where that source's dialect is unrecorded, or is one the writer can neither reuse nor synthesize, it resolves to the catalog default and charges `target.source-dialect-displaced`.

A `Strictness { pinned: bool, floor: Option<Severity>, codes: BTreeSet<NonBlankString> }` refuses an entry of a completed report where its severity is at least `floor`; where its code, as §3.2 or its codec's format specification spells it, is in `codes`; or where `pinned` holds, the entry carries a strict floor (§3.2), and its severity reaches it. `pinned` does not apply to a decode at `Container` depth, whose losses are by request; `floor` and `codes` do. Decode, write, and measurement (§3.5) take the same type. The sealed wrappers of decode and write apply it to the completed report, before any byte reaches the destination, and no backend refuses on a report entry. Its default refuses nothing. Only the sealed encode wrapper constructs a `StrictWriteRejection`. `ExportReport.synthesis_cause` holds `PatchDeclined { reason }` only.

### 3.5 Caller policy (CLI)

- `convert` writes by default and reports. It holds no refusal rule of its own: each flag below sets the decode's or the write's `Strictness` (§3.4, Refusals), so a library caller can refuse whatever `convert` refuses. `--reject-errors` adds `export:record.invalid` to the write's `codes`; `--reject-empty` adds `export:output.empty`; `--reject-lossy[=decode|export|any]` with `--reject-lossy-floor=info|warning|error|blocking` (default `info`) sets `floor` on the decode's `Strictness`, the write's, or both, and at `info` refuses a replay that carries undecoded records (`export:source.carried`); `--no-salvage` sets the decode's `pinned`. A refusal names the entry that refused it, with `strict_decode_rejected` at stage `decode` or `strict_export_rejected` at stage `export`.
- A check that cannot run to its end under the caller's ceilings is reported and does not stop the write. Under `--reject-errors` the conversion refuses with `resource_limit` at stage `check`, since the output cannot be shown free of Errors.
- `--reject-lossy=decode` judges this invocation's decode or the CADIR parse, whose report is `CadIr::read`'s (§3.3, Reading CADIR). A restored sidecar's report describes the earlier decode and never decides.
- A stale sidecar is ignored with `sidecar.stale`.
- `--container-only` decodes the container only. `convert` then writes the target from what the document holds, as for any document below the depth its writer requests (§3.4, Inputs): a same-format output replays the source (§3.4, Paths), and any other writes what the document states that the target can hold, with `export:output.empty` where that is nothing.
- `measure` measures what the document holds. Where the document's scope holds no `model` class, it reports no measured body and charges `measure:output.empty`, saying so. `measure --reject-empty` adds that code to the measurement's `Strictness`.
- A binary format is written to standard output only under `--binary-stdout`; a conversion that names no output file for one is refused with `binary_stdout_rejected` at stage `plan`. This is a destination guard, as an existing output without `--force` is.
- `--missing-states=geometry-true|history-true` (default `geometry-true`) sets `EncodeInput.missing_states`: the form a writer to a target that holds no feature without its state gives features whose states the target needs and the document lacks (§3.4). Every other target ignores it.
- A sub-full scope prints a note. `diff` reports `scope` and `unrepresented` changes. `PatchDeclined` reasons print once.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 negative verdict, 2 operational error.

### 3.6 Version policy

Readers accept exactly `ir_version: "11"`. Every earlier wire is refused with a message naming its difference from v11; all knowledge of earlier wires lives in `crates/cadmpeg-ir/src/document/legacy.rs`. There is no migration. Maintainers select the version for a release; after a release, any change to a product field's presence, name, type, units, parameterization, or invariant requires a new version. A reader ignores a member it does not know and reports it (§3.3, Reading CADIR).

## 4. Rule D: one fact, one place

**Kinds of duplication.**
- K1, a duplicate: the same fact stored twice. One copy is canonical; the other becomes a typed reference or is removed.
- K2, an evaluation cache: the IR declares the cache's source. `validate_neutral` checks agreement where in-IR arithmetic decides it (§10). Disagreement is legal when the evaluation's status is `Stale` or `Failed`.
- K3, independent facts that look alike: one resolver each.

**Shapes.**
- `Dimension<T, P = ParameterId> = Literal(T) | Parameter(P) | Negated(P)` for every value a parameter can drive: quantities, counts, booleans, and option enums (§5.14). A bound dimension stores no value of its own and binds a parameter of its own scope; `CadIr::dimension_value` resolves it. `Negated(p)` is the negative of `p`'s value for a signed quantity, and the complement for a boolean: sources store one quantity with opposite signs (NX measures an extrude's start limit and a revolve's start angle along the direction, every other format against it; SolidWorks stores a positive draft angle with an outward flag and a positive offset with a reverse flag), and the binding survives the sign. A writer whose format stores a flag writes the parameter and sets the flag. Process values are `ProcessDimension<T> = Dimension<T, ParamRef>`, which bind process or design parameters (§5.13, §7.7).
- `Expression<R = ParameterRef> = Neutral(Neutral<R>) | Source { dialect, tokens }` (§5.13). The neutral tree is typed and unit-checked, and keeps each literal's authored unit; `Source` keeps the source's text with references as tokens. The expression is canonical; the parameter's value is its cache. Dependencies derive from references.
- `DesignParameter { kind, definition: Expression | Driven | Assigned(program) | Unset, value }` (§5.12). `kind` is canonical over the value's quantity.
- Configurations are a base plus overrides (§5.11).
- Resolvers: `effective_display_color` (the colour of the statement that holds for the entity at its instance path and state: a display colour, or the `base_color` of an appearance; `None` where no statement holds, or where the appearance that holds states no base colour. Statements are made in the definitions along the path: the one that holds the entity, and each one that places it, out to the owner of the path's first occurrence. In the definition that holds the entity, its display colour is a statement on the entity, and its body's display colour one on its body. In each definition, a binding is a statement on its target where its `path` is the steps of the path from that definition to the target (`None` where the definition owns the target, or is the target) and its `state` the state that instance is read in (§8); and the appearance that an entry of a display arrangement in force there sets is a statement on the occurrence its `path` ends at, where that `path` is the steps of the path from that definition through that occurrence (§5.11). An entry that sets no appearance states no colour. A statement on a body, an occurrence, or a definition applies to the bodies and faces under it and to the cage of a body whose shell holds one (§5.6), and to an edge or a vertex only where its body has no faces (a wire body). Targets are ordered by nearness to the entity: the entity, then its body, then the definition that holds the entity, then each definition farther out along the path, to the owner of the path's first occurrence; an occurrence of the path is as near as the definition it places. On one target in one definition, an arrangement's appearance holds over a binding, a display colour over a binding, and of two bindings at one place the first in arena order. The definitions are taken in order, from the one that holds the entity outward; one that states nothing for the entity leaves the statement held. A statement of the definition taken can be held where none is held yet, where its `precedence` is `Outer`, or where its target is at least as near the entity as the target of the statement held (§8). Of the statements that can, the one on the nearest target is held from there on; where none can, the statement held stays. So in the definition that holds the entity the statement on the nearest target holds; an appearance bound to the entity at its path stands before the entity's display colour, which stands before one bound to it with `path: None`; and no statement of an inner definition shows through an `Outer` statement), `effective_visibility` (the AND of every display gate on the entity at its instance path and state: the `visible` of its holding body, mesh, or point cloud; the resolved `visible` of each occurrence of the path; the `visible` of each appearance binding on the entity or on its holding body at that path and state, or with `path: None`; and the `visible` of each presentation layer that lists the entity, its body, or an occurrence of the path, and of each ancestor of such a layer through `parent`. A `ViewPresentation` is no gate: it names a source object, not an entity), `effective_suppression` (true where an occurrence of the path resolves suppressed, or where the definition that owns the entity or a prototype that an occurrence of the path places is not `active` (§8.1): the instance is then out of the product, which is no display state; a writer writes it as suppression where its target holds suppression, and writes no instance where it does not), `effective_transform` (occurrence chain composed in document coordinates; `None` when any link states no placement). A tessellation whose `of` is `Definition` and a point cloud resolve through `effective_display_color`, `effective_visibility`, and `effective_suppression` as a body does: their own `color` and `visible` stand where a body's do, and an appearance bound to the tessellation stands where one bound to the body does. `effective_suppression`, `effective_visibility`, and `effective_transform` resolve each occurrence of a path, outermost first, through the configuration that applies to it: an occurrence reached through an ancestor resolves through the configuration that ancestor selects for its prototype (its resolved `OccurrenceDesign.configuration`, §5.1), and the scope's active configuration applies only where no ancestor selects one. Each occurrence's suppression, visibility, and placement is its base value (§8.1) resolved through that configuration and then through the arrangements in force in it (§5.11), then the nested overrides of the occurrences above it, base, per configuration, and per arrangement in force (§5.11, §8.1), applied innermost occurrence first, so where two occurrences above it state one field for it, the outer occurrence's value holds; its placement is then the pose its scope's current state states for it, where that configuration is the active one and the current state states one (§5.5). World placement is computed, never stored. An arrangement in force applies its `nested` entries: the arrangement a `nested` entry names is in force for the instance at its path, in place of the arrangement of that arrangement's kind that the occurrence would otherwise use (its `OccurrenceDesign.arrangements` entry, else the one in force in the configuration it uses, §5.11). An `Explode` arrangement's `moves` change no placement: `effective_transform` applies none, and a writer whose target holds exploded views writes them as such. A `ConfigurationRef::Named` selects no configuration the document holds, so the occurrences below resolve through the prototype scope's active configuration, as with no selection; an `ArrangementRef::Named` likewise selects none, and the instance uses the arrangement it would use without that entry.
- `SourceObjectAssociation` is identity only.
- A neutral `properties`, `native_options`, or `source_settings` map holds only source facts no typed field holds.

**Rulings.**

| Id | Duplication | Ruling |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | operation dimension fields vs an owned parameter | `Dimension<T>`; the parameter is canonical |
| D2 | `FeatureOperation::Native` options vs `DesignParameter` expressions | an option driven by an expression is `Dimension::Parameter`; native options hold no expression |
| D3 | a record's `native_options`, `source_settings`, or a `SourceAttribute` vs its typed fields | the typed field is canonical; no native map or attribute holds a fact a typed field holds, and no key is in both maps |
| D4 | a source feature record's child sequence (its text, the positions of its dimensions, its nested records) vs the neutral records | each fact has its neutral home: a parameter's owner is `DesignParameter.owner`, a nested feature's place is its container; the sequence is layout and stays in the feature's native record (§5.10) |
| D5 | expression vs value; measure vs geometry | the expression is canonical; the value and each `Measure.cached` are caches |
| D6 | `dependencies` vs identifiers | derived from `Reference` nodes and tokens; a cycle is a Warning, a dangling reference an Error |
| D7 | `display` vs modifiers inside the expression | `display` is canonical |
| D8 | owner name inside expression text | names hold no owner; writers render qualified names |
| D9 | solved sketch geometry vs constraints | constraints are canonical; the solved geometry is their cache |
| D10 | constraint value fields vs companion parameter fields | one `Dimension<T>` per pair |
| D11 | `SketchConstraint.driving` vs driven properties | `DesignParameter.definition` is canonical (`Driven`) |
| D12 | configuration overrides vs base | independent; an override replaces its base value in that configuration |
| D13 | a configuration restating the base | the stored design (features, parameters, occurrences and their `OccurrenceDesign`) is the base; a configuration states only its differences from its parent, or from the base; an occurrence's current values are its resolution through the configuration that applies to it (§4) and are not stored, except a current state's pose where it differs from that resolution (D54) |
| D14 | active feature states vs `Feature.suppressed` | as D13 |
| D15 | configuration copies of feature states | differences only |
| D16 | dimensions inside configuration definition overrides | a dimension difference is a parameter override; a definition override changes only non-dimensional structure |
| D17 | evaluated bodies per configuration | evaluations keyed by configuration (§5.4); the active configuration's current states are held in `CadIr.geometry` and the product definitions (§5.5) and have no evaluation |
| D18 | spreadsheet cell alias copies | the cell holds `address` and `parameter`; the alias is the parameter's name |
| D19 | colour | one source colour, one home: an Appearance and binding, or a display-colour field |
| D20 | visibility at body, mesh body, point cloud, occurrence, binding, layer | independent; `effective_visibility` |
| D21 | `SourceObjectAssociation` name, colour, visibility, layer | identity only; the rest go to their homes |
| D22 | `ViewPresentation.visible` vs a Visibility property | the typed field is canonical |
| D23 | procedural construction vs solved carrier | the construction is canonical; the end-point check of part 10 (Caches) applies |
| D24 | resolved values vs references | the reference is canonical; editing a referent marks dependent states `Stale` |
| D25 | occurrence transform vs body transform | world placement is computed |
| D26 | feature dependencies vs parameter edges | dependencies derive from definition references; parameter edges from expression references |
| D27 | browser-tree nodes vs container membership | containers are canonical; there is no tree-node operation |
| D28 | `ParameterPmi` vs `PmiAnnotation` | the annotation is canonical, its dimension's `nominal` a `Dimension<PmiValue>` (§8); the parameter has no `pmi` field |
| D29 | topology parent pointers vs child lists | the parent pointer is canonical: an unordered child list (a shell's faces, a body's regions) is derived from it and not stored; a child list whose order or classification carries meaning (a region's shells, a face's loops, a loop's coedges) is kept, with a reciprocity check (§5.6) |
| D30 | a joint's suppression and identity held by a feature and by a model record | the `Joint` feature is canonical: its suppression is `Feature.suppressed`, and a model record that targets a joint (a solver setting) names the feature's `FeatureId`; there is no `JointId` and no `assembly_joints` arena (§8) |
| D31 | a source control bound to one parameter | folded into the `Dimension<T>` when no other expression references the control |
| D32 | a stored-geometry feature's geometry vs the state after the feature | the state after the feature holds the geometry, as an evaluation or a current state; the feature names the bodies it contributes there and holds no topology of its own (§5.10) |
| D33 | a container's own result shape (FreeCAD Body `Shape` repeating its `Tip`) | the member's state is canonical; the repeat is removed |
| D34 | the state after a feature suppressed in a configuration vs the state before it (FreeCAD stores the suppressed feature's `Shape` as a copy of the state before it) | the feature is stateless in that configuration: it has no evaluation there, and the state after it is the state before it (§5.4); the stored copy is not emitted, and FreeCAD's `SuppressedShape`, a display cache, is removed |
| D35 | the state after a feature whose kind cannot change a state (a sketch, a datum, a feature that only generates other features) vs the state before it | the feature has no evaluation; the state after it is the state before it (§5.4) |
| D36 | a literal's authored unit vs its canonical value | the literal keeps value and unit as authored; canonical values exist only in caches |
| D37 | a `ParameterValue` quantity tag vs the declared kind | `kind` is canonical; `ParameterValue` holds the canonical number with no quantity tag |
| D38 | design, family, iPart, and configuration tables vs configurations | the configurations are canonical; the table layout is native. A scope with several independent table selectors (FreeCAD) states each selector as a parameter and each value it drives as an `if` expression on it, not as configurations (§5.14) |
| D39 | program assignments vs assigned parameters | `Assigned(program)` is canonical; a neutral program body's targets agree with it |
| D40 | translated neutral tree vs source text | the tree is canonical; the source text is native and re-emitted under W2 |
| D41 | construction inputs vs the source's construction `mode` | the inputs are canonical; an edit to the inputs removes the mode |
| D42 | a datum's value vs a source's display shape of the datum | the construction's `resolved` is the value; the display shape is removed |
| D43 | a rule selection with one unpropagated `Explicit` term and no exclusions vs a pick list | `Named` |
| D44 | a pick's resolved entities vs its target | the target is canonical; `Picked.resolved` is a K2 cache of the pick in its anchored state (§5.8) |
| D45 | a blend face's joined faces vs the face adjacency of its state | `Blend.between` holds them only where the source's name stores them; a decoder never derives them (§5.7); a transition's `against` is D59's |
| D46 | a name for every edge and vertex vs the names of the faces that meet there | a `Bounded` or `Meeting` pick resolves through its faces' names and the anchored state's adjacency; a name table holds an edge or vertex name only where the source stores one (§5.7) |
| D47 | a SolidWorks generated flexible configuration vs the occurrence's nested overrides | the nested overrides of the parent occurrence in the configuration that generated it (`OccurrenceOverride.nested`, or the base list where that configuration is the base); the generated configuration is no `DesignConfiguration`, and its name stays native (§5.11) |
| D48 | a minted parameter whose expression negates one reference vs `Dimension::Negated` | `Negated`; a decoder never mints such a parameter (§5.14) |
| D49 | the link between a material-removal design feature and the operation whose removal it is | the removal process state names the feature (`ProcessState.feature`); no design record names a process record (§7.9) |
| D50 | a construction's value in a configuration that is not active vs a rebuild from that configuration's inputs | the inputs are canonical; `Construction.resolved_in` keeps the value the source stores per configuration, a cache (K2) like `resolved` (§5.9) |
| D51 | a sketch constraint's solve status vs its operands | no constraint status is stored: a lost operand is a selection that does not resolve, and a satisfaction diagnosis is computed (§6.1) |
| D52 | a spline handle's direction vs a helper line that a relation dimensions | the helper line and its relations; the handle's `direction` is `None` (§6.1) |
| D53 | sheet-metal defaults that several features and bodies share vs a copy per feature | one `SheetMetalRule` record that features and `ApplyRule` features name; a feature field that is `None` takes the governing rule's value (§6.6) |
| D54 | an occurrence's placement in a state vs the placement its configuration resolves to | `delta.poses` and `CurrentState.poses` state a placement only where it differs from the resolved one (§5.4, §5.5) |
| D55 | a toolpath's frame vs its operation's resolved frame | the operation's frame rule is canonical; `Motions.frame` is its cache (K2) for the toolpath (§7.8) |
| D56 | a component's base placement vs the construction that binds it | `Occurrence.transform` is the one home of the value. `Place.placement` and `Place.scale` are the one home of its definition where the source stores a placement that can be bound and one scale composed with it (§6.7). `Container.placement` defines the occurrence of a FreeCAD PartDesign Body that an `App::Link` also places, and that occurrence has no `scale`. The placement's `resolved`, composed with `scale` where it is stated, is a cache (K2) of `Occurrence.transform` |
| D57 | a named set of occurrence placements, suppression, or display that the user activates independently of a configuration vs the configurations | an `Arrangement` record (§5.11) in every format that has one, whose overrides resolve over the configuration that applies; the arrangements in force are named per scope and per configuration (`active_arrangements`) and per occurrence (`OccurrenceDesign.arrangements`); the arrangement the source provides as its base, or the one active at decode where the source's arrangements are peers, states no overrides, and a configuration's active display state is stated by its appearance bindings; no configuration is multiplied to state an arrangement |
| D58 | a fit's `deviations` vs its designation and the nominal's value | the designation, `fit` with `mate`, is canonical. `Cell` deviations, the designation's cell in a published table the decoder holds, and `Unchecked` deviations, which no held table checks, are a cache (K2) of the designation at the nominal's base value: an edit of the value clears them, and a configuration that overrides the value does not restate them. `Own` deviations, which differ from that cell, are the source's own, and an edit keeps them (§5.12). A writer for a format that holds fits writes `fit` and `mate`, and writes the deviations as the target's override where they are `Own`, or where the target's own cell at the nominal differs from `Cell` or `Unchecked` deviations; where the target cannot hold that override it writes the deviations as the dimension's, keeps the designation where the target can, and charges `export:fit.restated` naming the parameter. A writer whose target holds no fit writes the deviations as the dimension's and charges `export:fit.restated` naming the parameter; where `deviations` is `None`, or a configuration's value differs from the base value under `Cell` or `Unchecked`, it writes no tolerance there and charges `export:fit.dropped` naming the parameter (§5.12) |
| D59 | a `RollingBall` or `SweptAround` transition's `against`, and a `radius` bound to the parameter of a round the corner continues, vs the corner's adjacency in the stored result | both are operands, not caches: `against` selects in the state entering the round, and the binding names the round's radius parameter (§6.4). A decoder whose source leaves the support or the continued round implicit states them from the stored corner where Rule H1's test holds, the binding inferred from the corner's seams (the face across the corner's seam, or across the seam of the round's own fillet) and the equal radius, and no edit clears them |
| D60 | a parameter's `decimals` vs the `decimals` of a PMI dimension whose `nominal` binds the parameter | a parameter's `decimals`, the key of the rule by decimals, is canonical, and a bound PMI dimension's `decimals` (§8) states its own only where it differs, and an equal one is a Warning (§5.12) |
| D61 | a parameter's `tolerance` vs the `tolerance` of a PMI dimension whose `nominal` binds the parameter | the parameter's `tolerance` is canonical; the PMI dimension states a `tolerance` of its own only where it differs from the parameter's, compared as values in one frame (on a `Negated` nominal, the dimension's `Deviations` `(lower, upper)` against the parameter's `(−upper, −lower)`), and an equal one is a Warning; a display form is no part of the value, and the rule holds whatever the arm, a basic, single-limit, or general tolerance included (§5.12, §8) |

**Editing a document.** The edit helpers are `set_dimension`, `set_parameter_expression`, `set_feature_definition`, `insert_member`, `remove_member`, and `set_active_configuration`. `CadIr::edit(&mut self, strictness: &Strictness) -> Result<Editor<'_>, EditError>` validates the document and returns an `Editor` over it, which holds the findings: `Editor::findings(&self) -> &[Finding]` gives the findings validation reports on the document as it now stands. It returns the validation report instead only where a finding reaches the caller's `strictness` (§3.4, Refusals; of `strictness`, only `floor` applies to a finding, and the default refuses none), and the `ResourceLimit` refusal where validation cannot run to its end under the resource ceilings it runs under (§2.5), which is no finding of the document. `Strictness::refuses_finding(&self, finding: &Finding) -> bool` states whether `floor` refuses a finding; `pinned` and `codes` name report entries. The helpers are the `Editor`'s methods, and the document is changed only through them while the `Editor` lives. Beyond the refusals stated for it, each helper refuses an edit whose result holds more Error findings of a rule on a record than the document held before it, a finding that names no record counting under its rule alone. It then returns the added findings and leaves the document unchanged. Where validation of the result cannot run to its end, it returns that refusal and leaves the document unchanged. So no edit makes the document hold an Error it did not hold. An Error the document held before the edit is reported with the `Editor`'s findings and refuses nothing; where the document was decoded, it is a defect of its decoder or of the rule (§1). No helper refuses an edit because its result would break a rule that is a Warning: a decoded document may hold that state, so an edit may reach it (a reference cycle; an integer-kind expression whose value is not whole, which then has no cache, §5.13). The resolvers (`dimension_value`, `is_stateless`, `effective_transform`, `effective_visibility`, `effective_suppression`, `effective_display_color`) are methods of `CadIr` and read any document, since a writer writes what the document holds (§3.4); on a document that holds an Error, a resolver returns an error where a definition it reads has no value (a configuration that is its own ancestor).

**Edit helpers.** `set_dimension`, `set_parameter_expression`, and `set_feature_definition` mark `Stale`:
- every evaluation and current state that depends on the edited feature or parameter, including `Tool` evaluations (§5.4, §5.5);
- the solve status of every sketch whose dimensions, parameters, or selection referents they edit (§6.1);
- every toolpath and process state whose operation reads geometry from such a state, through its own selections or those of a process record it takes geometry or values from (its machining features, its geometry groups and their parents, its setup's workpieces, stock, and fixtures, and its tool and holder where they select geometry), or depends on the edited parameter through a `ParamRef::Design` binding or reference of the operation or of a process parameter one of those records owns, and the later process states and modifier toolpaths that §7.9 names.

After the edit they recompute the cache of every dependent `Neutral` expression that has no uncached measure, and clear every dependent cache they cannot recompute, including one whose evaluation fails or has no value (§5.13): `DesignParameter.value`, the `Cell` and `Unchecked` deviations of every `Tolerance::Fit` whose nominal is the edited parameter, the parameter's own and each bound PMI dimension's (D58), `Measure.cached`, `ParameterOverride.value`, the process parameter values that depend on a design parameter through `ParamRef::Design` (each the cache of its expression in the active configuration of its setup's scope, §7.1, a design reference reading its cache for that configuration as §5.13 states), every `Choice` value one of whose `parameters` does, and the `resolved` of every `Transformation` one of whose steps binds the edited parameter (§6.5). A `ParameterOverride` with no `expression` whose `value` they clear states nothing, so they remove it (§5.11). A writer then never writes a stale cache as a value (§5.13).

`set_dimension(p, v)` replaces the definition of design parameter `p` with the one-literal expression `v`: for a quantity kind a number in its authored unit, a unit of that quantity (a negative value as `-` over its magnitude, §5.13); for an integer kind a whole number with no unit; a Boolean; or a text (an enumerator's wire name where an option binds `p`, §5.14). It sets the base definition. It writes no configuration's or arrangement's override. The override is then as the sentence above states: its value is recomputed, or it is removed where it states no expression and the value is cleared (D12). On a parameter that is `Driven`, `Assigned`, or has references it returns `DrivenParameter` with its drivers (an expression with references is replaced by `set_parameter_expression`, which states the new definition), and on a value that is not of `p`'s kind `KindMismatch`: a number of another quantity, a number with a unit or a fraction for an integer kind, or another variant. A `Native`-kind parameter has no neutral literal, so every value is refused. Edits to process records mark process states and toolpaths as §7.9 states.

`insert_member(c, i, records)` takes `records`, a `Design` that holds one new member (a feature, or a container with its members and theirs) and the records they own, and nothing else. It adds them to the document and makes that member a member of container `c`, at index `i` of an ordered container; it refuses where the document already holds one of their ids. `remove_member(m)` deletes `m` from the document with what it owns: where `m` is a container, every member under it; the sketches and spatial sketches whose `owner` is a deleted feature, with their entities and constraints (§6.1), and the sheet a deleted feature's `Spreadsheet` operation names (§5.12); the parameters whose `owner` is a deleted feature or container, and the programs whose `owner` is a deleted feature; the occurrences a deleted feature creates (§6.7, Existence), each removed from the `occurrences` of the definition that owns it, with its `OccurrenceDesign`, and every override, pose, `members` entry, and instance-body entry, in the document and in each evaluation it keeps, that is keyed by a deleted occurrence or by a path through one, with the instance bodies that only such an entry lists and the records only they reach; and every other override, pose, and instance-body entry keyed by a deleted record. It refuses, returning `Referenced` with the referring records, where a record it keeps names a deleted record by id (a `ParameterRef`, a bound `Dimension`, a `Datum`, `Feature`, `FeatureResult`, `Sketch`, or sketch-entity pick, a `Principal` pick of a deleted container's origin, a `Link`, a `ReferenceTarget::Feature`, a `driven_by`, a process state's `feature`, an occurrence path), since a dangling id is an Error (D6). A definition that a deleted occurrence placed is kept; an `Embedded` one that no kept occurrence places is spanned by the scope of its file (§5.1). A pick that resolves through a name mentioning a deleted record (a feature, a container, or an entity of a deleted sketch or spatial sketch) stays, and no longer resolves (D51). Either edit marks `Stale` every evaluation and current state at or after `m`'s position in an ordered container (§5.3), and every one that depends on a feature at or after it; in an unordered container, which has no order, every one that depends on a deleted member. A current state at the unstated rollback of an ordered container counts as at or after each of its members. Removal also deletes the evaluations keyed by a deleted member (`of` is `State(After(x))` or `Tool(x)`) and rebases the evaluations and process states based on them so that their resolved states are unchanged. It deletes each model-class record all of whose targets lie in geometry the removal deletes: the extent of a deleted current state, or a deleted evaluation (a tessellation of a deleted body, an appearance binding or an attribute on it, a PMI annotation on its entities alone). A model-class target whose `state` names a deleted evaluation lies in that evaluation, and no retarget of a position (below) moves it: a tessellation depicts the state it was stored for, and a binding or an annotation was stated of that state. It deletes the tessellations a removed `Stored` feature names, and removes the deleted entities from each presentation layer's `items`. It refuses, returning `Referenced` with the referring records, where any other record it keeps names a deleted record by id or targets deleted geometry (a PMI annotation or a declared measure that also targets geometry the document keeps, a drawing reference). In each state it keeps, a name-table entry whose name mentions a deleted record, as above, loses that name and keeps its `native`, and an entry left with neither is removed: no feature of the document now produced the entity (§5.7). These are the resolved tables of the kept states. An evaluation's `delta.names` states each as a difference from its base's resolved table, as cleaned: `None` for an entity whose entry the base holds and the state does not, the state's entry where it differs from the base's, and no key where they agree (§5.4). Removal rewrites only the entries of entities whose resolved entry it changes. In an ordered container it retargets every other position that names a deleted member, or the `Start` of a deleted container (a `Pinned` anchor, the position of a current state it keeps), to the position before `m` (§5.3), and retargets `Rollback::Before(m)` to the member after `m`, or to `End` where `m` is the last member. An unstated rollback stays unstated. A folder of `m`'s container keeps its other members, and one left with no member is removed. In an unordered container, which has no position before a member (§5.3), removal removes the result that only each deleted member produced. For each deleted member `x` that has its own result (§5.3), it rebases every evaluation and process state whose base is `StateBase::Current(After(x))` so that its resolved state is unchanged, and then deletes the current state at `After(x)` with the part of its extent that no other current state's extent and no unproduced body holds: its bodies and the records only they reach (§5.6), their name entries, their owner entries, their instance-body entries, and its poses, as `set_active_configuration` removes an outgoing extent. It re-anchors every selection anchored `Pinned(After(x))` to `Current` (§5.8) and clears the `resolved` cache of every pick that lists a deleted record; a pick that named an entity of the deleted result no longer resolves (D51). Removing a container also deletes, in the same way, each current state at a position inside it or at `After(Container(d))` for the container or a container under it, since a container's states are its own (§5.2): such a state is deleted, and no retarget moves it to another position. Removal treats every other position inside the container as one that names the container. Where a removed container `c` is ordered and a member of an unordered container, it has no result of its own there, and its state at its rollback position stands for it outside it (§5.3): removal re-anchors to `Current` (§5.8) every selection pinned to `After(Container(c))` or to a position inside `c`, as it does one pinned to a deleted member's own result, and clears the `resolved` cache of every pick that lists a deleted record; a pick that named an entity of one of `c`'s states no longer resolves (D51).

`set_active_configuration(scope, c)` changes which configuration the current geometry holds for one scope, and keeps every state the document holds. It marks no toolpath and no process state `Stale`: a toolpath or process state keyed by a configuration stays that configuration's, and one with `configuration: None` is of every configuration (§7.8, §7.9). For each current state of that scope, it exchanges only that state's extent (§5.5): its bodies and the records they reach, their names, owners, and instance bodies, and its poses. The geometry, names, and records of other scopes and of the scope's other current states are untouched. So are the scope's unproduced bodies (§5.5).
- it writes the outgoing extent into an evaluation of the outgoing configuration at that current state's position;
- it removes the outgoing bodies and the records only they reach from `CadIr.geometry`, their entries from `Design.names`, their owner entries from the product definitions' `bodies`, and their instance-body entries, and installs the incoming configuration's evaluation of that position in their place: its bodies and records into `CadIr.geometry`, its names into `Design.names`, its owners into `ProductDefinition.bodies`, its instance bodies onto the definitions that own them, and its poses into the current state's `poses`; it lists the installed bodies in the current state and removes that evaluation. Where the document holds no evaluation of that position for `c`, it keeps the current state and marks it `Stale`;
- it rewrites the `state` of the model-class targets (§8) of the extents it exchanges, of the tessellations of their bodies, and of the `Definition` tessellations of the definitions whose geometry it exchanges: a target or tessellation into the outgoing extent, and a `Definition` tessellation with `state: None`, takes the `StateRef` of the outgoing configuration's evaluation that the first step wrote, and one into the installed evaluation takes `state: None`;
- for each construction of the scope's design whose `resolved` is a cache (one with inputs or steps), it moves `resolved` into `resolved_in` under the outgoing configuration, and takes the incoming configuration's entry as `resolved`, or clears `resolved` where `resolved_in` has none (§5.9);
- it recomputes, for `c`, the process parameter values that depend on a design parameter through `ParamRef::Design` (Edit helpers, above), and clears each it cannot recompute;
- it rebases every evaluation whose base is `StateBase::Current(p)` for an exchanged position `p`, and every process state based on one, so that its resolved state is unchanged, and sets `active_configuration` to `c`; current occurrence values of the scope then resolve through `c` and the arrangements in force in it (§5.11).

## 5. The design layer

```rust
pub struct Design {
    pub scopes: Vec<DesignScope>,
    pub containers: Vec<Container>,
    pub features: Vec<Feature>,
    pub sketches: Vec<Sketch>,
    pub sketch_entities: Vec<SketchEntity<Planar>>,
    pub sketch_constraints: Vec<SketchConstraint<Planar>>,
    pub spatial_sketches: Vec<SpatialSketch>,
    pub spatial_sketch_entities: Vec<SketchEntity<Spatial>>,
    pub spatial_sketch_constraints: Vec<SketchConstraint<Spatial>>,
    pub parameters: Vec<DesignParameter>,
    pub spreadsheets: Vec<Spreadsheet>,
    pub sheet_metal_rules: Vec<SheetMetalRule>,
    pub programs: Vec<ParameterProgram>,
    pub configurations: Vec<DesignConfiguration>,
    pub arrangements: Vec<Arrangement>,
    pub publications: Vec<Publication>,
    pub evaluations: Vec<Evaluation>,
    pub names: NameTable,
}
pub struct DesignScope {
    pub definition: ProductDefinitionId,
    pub roots: Vec<ContainerId>,
    pub active_configuration: Option<ConfigurationId>,
    pub active_arrangements: BTreeSet<ArrangementId>,
    pub occurrences: BTreeMap<OccurrenceId, OccurrenceDesign>,
    pub current: Vec<CurrentState>,
    pub unproduced: BTreeSet<BodyId>,
}
pub struct OccurrenceDesign {
    pub configuration: Option<ConfigurationRef>,
    pub arrangements: Vec<ArrangementRef>,
    pub grounded: Option<bool>,
    pub flexible: Option<bool>,
    pub parameters: BTreeMap<ParameterId, ParameterOverride>,
}
pub enum ConfigurationRef { Local(ConfigurationId), Named(NonBlankString) }
```

### 5.1 Scopes

A design scope is the design of one product definition: its history, parameters, configurations, and current states. A source document that keeps its own history is one scope (a SolidWorks, Inventor, NX, Creo, or CATIA part or assembly file; a FreeCAD document). A Fusion document is one scope at its root component, whose single timeline holds the features of every component.

- A document holds one scope per product definition that has a design, and at most one per definition. A decode of an assembly with its component files (§3.1) yields one scope per file. A definition that no scope spans (below) has no design in this document: a geometry-only component file, or an external document that was not read (§8.1).
- A scope holds a design: a root container that has a member, a parameter, program, sheet-metal rule, configuration, arrangement, or publication that names it, an `occurrences` entry, or a setup that names it (§7.1). A definition for which the document holds none of these, only bodies that no member produces, has no scope: its geometry stands without a design, as a geometry-only file's does (§1). A decoder that reads no design record of a definition states no scope for it, and no container to hold its bodies.
- Root containers, parameters, parameter programs, sheet-metal rules, and configurations each name their scope (`scope: ProductDefinitionId`). Parameter names are unique among the parameters of one scope with one owner (SolidWorks repeats `D1` in every sketch).
- A scope spans its own definition and every `Embedded` definition with no scope of its own that is placed below it: the prototype of an occurrence that a spanned definition owns (`ProductDefinition.occurrences`, §8.1), the walk stopping at a definition stored as `File` or `External` and at one with a scope. The scope of a `File` definition also spans every `Embedded` definition with no scope that its file stores and no occurrence places (the file whose definition key qualifies the definition's id, and the root file where none does, §2.2), and the definitions placed below each of them. A Fusion component and a FreeCAD object that an `App::Link` of its own document places are spanned so, and so are the products a STEP file or a USD stage holds below its scope of joints (§6.7); a component file's definition is not. No definition is spanned by two scopes. A scope spans several definitions where it spans any besides its own. `Feature.component` names the definition under which the source lists a feature of a scope that spans several definitions; the root component is named explicitly, and `None` states that the decoder did not establish the owner. In a scope that spans one definition, `component` is `None`. A writer that files features by definition never files a feature with no established owner under the root: it charges a loss naming the feature.
- A feature may select and change bodies of any definition its selections reach (§5.8). A feature of a scope that spans several definitions may name an occurrence owned by any definition the scope spans (a Fusion insert of component A into component B, a joint between occurrences of B).
- `occurrences` holds the design state of an occurrence owned by a definition the scope spans. These are base values (D13); an occurrence's current values are their resolution through the configuration that applies to it (§4, §5.11). `configuration` is the configuration of its prototype that the occurrence uses (a Creo family-table instance, an Inventor model state, a SolidWorks referenced configuration); `Named` names a configuration of a prototype that has no scope here, or that the prototype no longer has. With no entry the occurrence uses its prototype's active configuration. The occurrences inside its prototype then resolve through the configuration it uses, not through the prototype scope's active configuration (§4). `arrangements` names the arrangements of its prototype that the occurrence uses, at most one of each kind (an NX component's arrangement in use); with none of a kind it uses the arrangement of that kind in force in the configuration it uses (§5.11). `grounded` states that the source fixes the occurrence in place. `flexible` states that the parent solves the occurrence's nested placements from the sub-assembly's own joints; its nested overrides (§8.1), base and per configuration (§5.11), are then the cache of that solution in each configuration.
- `parameters` gives parameters of the prototype values of their own in this occurrence alone (Creo flexible components and NX deformable parts vary dimensions per occurrence). Each key is a parameter of the prototype's scope, and its `ParameterOverride` replaces that parameter's expression, or states the value the source caches, in this occurrence as a configuration's override does (§5.11). The occurrence's geometry under those values is its instance bodies (§8.1). A CATIA product relation that drives a child parameter through an occurrence path is an expression with `ParameterRef.through` (§5.13), not an entry here. A writer whose target has no per-occurrence values writes a configuration of the prototype with the overridden values, which the occurrence selects, where the target has configurations; otherwise a copy of the prototype's definition with those values, which the occurrence places in its stead, which is an output the writer creates where definitions are files, and which no longer follows an edit of the prototype (§3.4, Lowering).

### 5.2 Containers

```rust
pub enum Container {
    Ordered   { id: ContainerId, kind: OrderedKind, members: Vec<Member>, folders: Vec<Folder>, rollback: Option<Rollback>, placement: Option<Construction<Frame>> },
    Unordered { id: ContainerId, kind: UnorderedKind, members: BTreeSet<Member> },
}
pub enum Member { Feature(FeatureId), Container(ContainerId) }
pub enum OrderedKind { Timeline, Body, GeometricalSet }
pub enum UnorderedKind { GeometricalSet, Group }
pub struct Folder { pub name: Option<String>, pub first: u32, pub last: u32 }
pub enum Rollback { End, Before(Member) }
```

History is a graph of features with containers inside it.

| Source | Containers |
|---|---|
| Creo, NX, SolidWorks | one ordered `Timeline` per scope; SolidWorks' rollback bar is `Rollback::Before`; SolidWorks FeatureManager folders are `Folder`s. A Creo assembly's timeline holds its component placements and assembly features in regeneration order |
| Inventor | one ordered `Timeline`, with the end-of-part marker as `Rollback::Before`; a sheet-metal flat pattern is a second root `Timeline`; the Blocks folder is a root unordered `Group` (§6.1) |
| Fusion | one ordered `Timeline` per timeline in the design stream that holds an item, each a root of the document's scope; a component's empty timeline (every component stores one, and only the root's holds items) is native, and the F3D writer regenerates it; timeline groups are `Folder`s. A design stream that holds no timeline item has no ordered container: its sketches and construction geometry are members of one root unordered `Group`, and its bodies are unproduced (§5.5). A stream that holds only such bodies has no scope (§5.1). |
| CATIA | a part's top-level bodies, ordered geometrical sets, and geometrical sets are roots of its scope, listed as the part lists them: ordered `Body` containers, ordered `GeometricalSet`s, and unordered `GeometricalSet`s. The features the part lists outside every set (its xy, yz, and zx planes among them, §6.2) are members of one root unordered `Group`, the part's own, which is listed first. A set that the part stores inside another is a member of it. A Boolean feature selects another body's result. The part's one in-work object is the `rollback` of the body or ordered geometrical set that lists it as a member: `Before` the member after it, or `End` where it is that set's last member; where the in-work object is itself a body or an ordered geometrical set, that set's `rollback` is `End` (part 11) |
| FreeCAD | each PartDesign Body an ordered `Body` with `Tip` as `Rollback`; Part workbench objects, and `App::Link` objects as `Place` features (§6.7), members of an unordered `Group` |
| Rhino | history records members of one unordered `Group`; an object that no history record lists among its descendants is unproduced (§5.5); so is an object that two or more records list among their descendants: a body belongs to one state (§5.5) and the file names no one record as its producer, so the decoder lists it as unproduced and charges a loss naming the object and the records (part 11) |

- Membership lives only in containers. Every feature and container is a member of exactly one container or is a root of exactly one scope; containers form a tree.
- Where a source lists a scope's root containers in one list (a CATIA part's list of its sets), `roots` keeps that order; otherwise their order states nothing. It is display order and scopes nothing: no state, position, or rule depends on it, and a scope that loses a root to a given-up part keeps its other roots in their order (§3.3).
- Sketches, datums, component placements, and joints are features (§6) and so are members of a container, with a place in its order where it is ordered.
- Dependencies derive from definition references (D26) and cross containers and scopes freely. A dependency cycle is legal in the document and reported as a Warning (FreeCAD and Rhino store cycles).
- `rollback` is how far the source builds the container: `End` through its last member, `Before(m)` before member `m`, so that `m` and every member after it are not built. `Rollback::Before(m)` names a member of its container. `None` where no stored fact the decoder read fixes it (§3.1). A decoder states the rollback where it reads the source's marker (FreeCAD `Tip`, the Inventor end-of-part marker, the CATIA in-work object) or another stored fact that fixes it, and a decoder of a format established to save every container built through its end states `End`; it never fills one it did not read (§2.4). A writer writes an unstated rollback as its target's own default (§3.4). An unordered container has no rollback and no order.
- `kind` says what the container is in its source (table above). A `Timeline` is a history of any number of bodies. A `Body` is an ordered container whose solid features build one body and act on it (`targets`, §6); in a CATIA body, wireframe and surface features also have results in its states. An ordered `GeometricalSet` is a CATIA ordered geometrical set, whose features build wireframe and surfaces in order, each result a body of its own; it is typed from Dassault's pages Managing Ordered Geometrical Sets and Order and Absorption Concepts. An unordered `GeometricalSet` is a CATIA geometrical set, and a `Group` any other set of independent members.
- `placement` is the placement a source applies to the whole of an ordered container's result (a FreeCAD PartDesign Body's `Placement`), as a construction whose components can be bound. An ordered container's states are in its local frame: its members' operands, picks, sketch frames, and `Principal { container }` values read them there (FreeCAD stores a Body's feature shapes in Body coordinates). `placement` maps that frame into the definition's. A member reads the frame of the nearest ordered container that holds it, and that container's own `placement` alone maps the frame into the definition's; where that `placement` is `None`, the frame is the definition's, also inside a placed ordered container. `Body.transform` (§5.6) holds the placement's resolved value on each body of the container's states, in the current geometry and in every evaluation alike (resolved in the evaluation's configuration), and a geometry writer applies it; the construction's `resolved` is the cache of that `Body.transform` in the current geometry. A reference that reaches the result through the container reads it under the placement: an operand or a pick at `After(Container(c))` (§5.3), and, where no `App::Link` places the container's object, a process pick with `workpiece: None` (part 7). A workpiece with a `placement` reads it under that placement instead (§7.1). Where an `App::Link` places the container's object, the object is a definition of its own whose bodies have no `Body.transform`, `placement` defines the transform of the object's own occurrence, and `resolved` is the cache of that `Occurrence.transform`; a selection from outside the object reaches its result through that occurrence or the object's definition (§6.7). `None` where the source has none.
- An ordered container carries its own origin where the source stores origin entities that belong to the container: a FreeCAD PartDesign Body, whose `Origin` holds its planes, axes, and point in the Body's local frame. A container whose source stores none (a CATIA body, a part's timeline) carries none: its members read their definition's origin, or its origin features (§6.2).
- A container scopes a state: an ordered container builds one cumulative state, and a member of an unordered container has its own result where §5.3 gives it one. A `Folder` is a display grouping of a contiguous run of an ordered container's members (`first` to `last`, by index); it scopes no state, has no position, and has no rollback. Folders of one container nest or are disjoint.

### 5.3 Positions

```rust
pub enum Position { Start(ContainerId), After(Member) }
```

A position is a state boundary. `Start(c)` is the state entering ordered container `c` before its first member. `After(m)` is the state leaving member `m`: in an ordered container, the cumulative state after `m`; in an unordered container, `m`'s own result. A feature that is a member of an unordered container has its own result in a configuration unless it is stateless there (§5.4) or its operation there is a `Place`, `PlaceSet`, `Joint`, `RigidGroup`, `ComponentPattern`, or `MirrorComponents`: the container's members produce the effect of those six together, as the occurrences' base placements and existence (§6.7), and none of them has a state of its own.
