A source's flip of the offset is the distance's sign, bound through `Dimension::Negated` where a parameter drives it (SolidWorks offset surface flip). `Move` changes the faces in place (Fusion OffsetFaces, NX offset face, SolidWorks move face by offset). `Copy` makes a new body with its output: a sheet (an offset surface: CATIA offset, SolidWorks offset surface, Fusion SurfaceOffset, NX offset, Creo offset, Inventor), or a solid where the copy closes (FreeCAD `Part::Offset` of every face of a solid). Faces excluded from an offset of a whole sheet (CATIA `TrickyFaces`) are the `excluded` terms of a `Rule` selection whose term is `Of { kind: Face }` seeded by the sheet: the result is the offset of the remaining faces.

#### Draft

```rust
pub struct Draft {
    pub sets: Vec<DraftSet>,
    pub pull: Option<Construction<Direction>>,
    pub neutral: Option<Construction<Plane>>,
    pub parting: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub steps: Option<StepFaces>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub struct DraftSet { pub faces: Option<SetSelection>, pub fixed: Option<SetSelection>, pub angle: Option<DraftAngle> }
pub enum DraftAngle {
    One(Dimension<SlopeAngle>),
    Two { first: Dimension<SlopeAngle>, second: Dimension<SlopeAngle> },
    Symmetric(Dimension<SlopeAngle>),
    Variable(Stations<SlopeAngle>),
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum StepFaces { Tapered, Perpendicular }
```

- A draft tilts the faces of each set by its angle relative to the pull direction. Several sets carry several angles in one feature (NX face-set angle list).
- What stays fixed decides the draft kind. `neutral` is a fixed plane: a datum, a planar face, or an origin plane. `DraftSet.fixed` holds the edges of that set that stay fixed (Inventor fixed edges, NX edge draft). `parting` is the element along which faces split and draft away on each side: edges, curves, a surface, or a plane (SolidWorks parting line, CATIA `Parting`, NX parting edges).
- `pull` is the pull direction. Where the source derives it from the neutral plane, the construction holds one `Whole` `Perpendicular` input on that plane. A source's flip of the pull is a `Flip` step of the construction (Fusion flipped, FreeCAD `Reversed`, the SolidWorks face draft's reverse direction), or the signed direction the source stores. A face draft has no material-side choice: SolidWorks "draft outward" belongs to extrusions, ribs, holes, and core features, where it is the sign of the draft angle (§6.3).
- `steps` makes a parting-line draft a step draft: each drafted face is one face rotated about the plane the pull direction is normal to, so a parting line with a segment in that plane on each drafted face and its other segments along the pull leaves small step faces between the segments; `Tapered` steps are generated as the tapered faces are, and `Perpendicular` steps are perpendicular to the original face (SolidWorks step draft: API `IDraftFeatureData2.StepType` and the Parting Line with Step Draft help). A writer whose target has no step draft writes a parting-line draft and charges a loss naming the feature.
- `Two` drafts the faces on the side of the neutral or parting element that the pull direction points to by `first`, and on the other side by `second`; `Symmetric` uses one angle on both sides (Fusion modes 2 and 3, CATIA `Angle2`, NX both sides). `Variable` varies the angle along the fixed chain (CATIA `Variation`, NX variable angle points).
- `faces` is `None` where the source drafts the faces adjacent to `fixed` edges without stating them. Face propagation is a selection rule (SolidWorks along tangent, Fusion tangent chain).
- The operands, not a source's mode code, carry the draft kind: fixed edges are `DraftSet.fixed`, a plane is `neutral`, and a parting tool is `parting` (Inventor face-draft mode 0 fills an edge collection, the fixed edges, and mode 2 an origin or work plane, the neutral plane). Inventor's mode 3 names a model face by a face item; a fixed plane and a parting tool give the same result where no drafted face crosses the plane, and no stored file known to the project settles which mode 3 is, so mode 3 keeps its mode and face as native options of the draft (Rule N case (a), part 11).

#### Hole

```rust
pub struct Hole {
    pub positions: HolePositions,
    pub start: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub direction: Option<Construction<Direction>>,
    pub shape: HoleShape,
    pub extent: Option<Limit<Length>>,
    pub standard: Option<StandardSize>,
    pub thread: Option<ThreadSpec>,
    pub targets: Option<Targets>,
    pub series: Vec<SeriesStage>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub struct SeriesStage { pub parts: SetSelection, pub hole: StageHole }
pub enum StageHole {
    /// The stage's own hole, which the assembly feature cuts in each picked part.
    Stated { shape: HoleShape, extent: Option<Limit<Length>>, standard: Option<StandardSize>, thread: Option<ThreadSpec> },
    /// The stage is a hole feature of the picked part's own history, placed by the series, which cuts nothing itself.
    PartFeature(FeatureId),
}
pub enum HolePositions {
    Points { points: OrderedSelection, centers: Option<BTreeSet<CenterSource>> },
    Placed(Vec<Construction<Point>>),
}
pub enum CenterSource { Points, Circles, Arcs }
pub enum HoleShape {
    Bore(Bore),
    Revolved(ProfileRef),
    Slot { bore: Bore, length: Dimension<PositiveLength>, measure: Option<SlotLength>, direction: Construction<Direction> },
}
pub enum SlotLength { CenterToCenter, TangentToTangent }
pub struct Bore {
    pub diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>,
    pub head: Option<HoleHead>,
    pub taper: Option<Dimension<SlopeAngle>>,
    pub bottom: Option<HoleBottom>,
    pub near_chamfer: Option<Cone>,
    pub neck_chamfer: Option<Cone>,
    pub far_chamfer: Option<Cone>,
}
pub enum HoleHead {
    Plain,
    Counterbore { diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, depth: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>> },
    Countersink(Cone),
    Counterdrill { diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, depth: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, angle: Option<Dimension<InteriorAngle>> },
    Spotface { diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, depth: Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub struct Cone { pub diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, pub depth: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>, pub angle: Option<Dimension<InteriorAngle>> }
pub enum HoleBottom { Flat, DrillPoint { angle: Option<Dimension<InteriorAngle>>, depth_to: Option<DepthTo> }, Trimmed, Native(NonBlankString) }
pub enum DepthTo { Shoulder, Tip }
pub struct StandardSize {
    pub standard: NonBlankString,
    pub kind: Option<NonBlankString>,
    pub size: Option<Dimension<NonBlankString>>,
    pub class: Option<NonBlankString>,
}
```

- One hole feature drills one shape at every position. `Points` picks sketch points, vertices, or datum points, or a whole sketch whose points are positions (SolidWorks placement sketch, Fusion, Inventor, and NX sketch points, CATIA positioning sketch). `centers` states which geometry of a whole-sketch pick yields positions (FreeCAD `BaseProfileType`).
- `Placed` holds one construction per position that relates it to references with dimensions: two distances from edges or datums, concentric with a cylindrical face or edge (`Center`), or on a datum point (Creo placement instructions, Inventor placement record). A position that is one picked point is a `Points` pick.
- `start` selects the face the holes start on (Creo placement surface, Fusion and CATIA support face); a `Placed` construction states no `Coincident` input for it. `direction` is the drilling direction, normal to `start` unless a reference says otherwise (NX projection direction, CATIA `Direction`); a source's flip is a `Flip` step of the construction.
- `extent` is §6's one-sided limit: blind, through all, up to next, through the body, or up to a face, plane, body, or vertex with an offset (CATIA `HoleLimit`, Creo `depth_choice`, Inventor to face). The depth runs from the start face to the shoulder unless `DepthTo::Tip` says otherwise. Fusion stores extent control 1 for every extent that is not a distance and tells them apart by the hole's last construction group: one whole-body recipe after the start faces is `ThroughAll`, and a face recipe is `ToGeometry` on that face; the `ToGeometry` reading rests on the stored operand (part 11). A control-1 hole of another group shape is `Limit::Native("f3d:hole_extent")`.
- `Bore` states the bore from entry to bottom. `head` is the entry recess; `Plain` states that there is none. `Spotface` is a recess of `diameter` and `depth`, like a counterbore's, from whose floor the hole's `extent` and its thread depth are measured, where a counterbore's are measured from `start` (Inventor: "Measurement of the hole and thread depth starts from the bottom surface of the spotface", To Create Holes help and API `HoleFeature.SetSpotFace`). Where its depth is measured on a start face that is not flat is part 11's question. A writer whose target has no spotface writes a `Counterbore` of its diameter and depth and adds that depth to the hole's `extent` and to a blind thread's length, exact on a flat start face. `Slot` sweeps the hole's section, its head included, along a segment centred on its position point in `direction`, so its end arcs have the bore's radius and a head's arcs are concentric with them; `measure` states how `length` is read, the end-arc centres lying `length` apart (`CenterToCenter`) or `length` less the bore diameter apart (`TangentToTangent`). `direction` runs from the position point toward the first end point (SolidWorks Hole Wizard slots: each stores its position point and two end points at ±`length`/2 on one line, so no default direction applies). Which stored field holds the scheme is typed, carrier unread (part 11): until it is read the SolidWorks decoder reads the scheme from the end arcs of the stored state, marked `derived`, and states `None` where the state does not hold them. `measure` decides how `length` is read, so where it is `None` a writer of another codec does not write the slot and charges a loss naming the feature (§2.4). A writer whose target has no slot hole writes a cut of the slot's outline and a second cut for its head, two geometry features under §3.4's rules for a construction, and charges `export:feature.lowered`. NX hole relief stays native, since no stored file known to the project shows what one builds (Rule N case (a), part 11). The relief is a sub-object that NX writes in the hole package of threaded and countersunk holes and of no simple or counterbored one: an off flag and references to expressions. Every reference is an external row of the feature section that names an expression, and none names a face, an edge, a body, or an enumeration. A threaded hole's relief names three expressions, a length, an angle, and a length, each a bare number. A countersunk hole's names one length. The flag `01` is the value the sibling chamfer object stores when its chamfer is off; the values are those the hole form supplies and nothing is built from them; which threaded length is a depth and which a diameter is not established, and no field is named for either. The decoder keeps the flag as `nx:hole_relief` and the references, in stored order, as `nx:hole_relief.1` to `nx:hole_relief.3` in the hole's `native_options`, each a length or an angle whose value is its expression's parameter, so the relief's values stay editable, and it states no relief geometry. An NX hole series (`HoleSeries`), one hole through a stack of bodies with start, middle, and end hole data of its own, keeps that stage data as the native option `nx:hole_series`: no stored file known to the project declares series hole data, and Siemens' pages that would state its stages are behind a login, so what each NX stage holds is not established (Rule N case (a), part 11). `Trimmed` ends the bore on the face that bounds its extent, which forms the bottom, with no cone or cap of its own inside the material. CATIA stores the bottom as `CatHoleBottomType` + 1: 1 is `Flat`, 2 is `DrillPoint`, and 3 is `Trimmed` (on limit codes 4, 7, 5, and 6 and never on the depth limit). On a bounding face normal to the axis, ending on the face and a flat bottom normal to the axis give one result, so the bottom on a face inclined to the axis is open (part 11). A `Counterdrill` is a cylindrical recess of `diameter` and `depth` entered through a cone of included `angle` (CATIA counterdrilled, FreeCAD `Counterdrill`). `taper` makes the bore conical (CATIA, NX, FreeCAD). `near_chamfer` is a countersink at the entry above the head, `neck_chamfer` one between the head and the bore, `far_chamfer` one at the exit (SolidWorks near-side, under-head, and far-side countersinks; NX start, neck, and end chamfers).
- A `Cone` holds the two of diameter, depth, and included angle that the source drives (CATIA `Hole_CSMode`); the third is absent.
- `Revolved` is a sketched hole: the profile revolves about the hole axis (Creo).
- `standard` sizes a clearance or drilled hole from a standard: standard, fastener kind, size, fit class (SolidWorks Hole Wizard, NX screw clearance and drill size, FreeCAD). A tapped hole's designation is `thread.standard`, and a hole with a `thread` states no `standard`; where a `Thread` feature threads the bore (a child thread with a feature node of its own, below), the designation is that feature's `spec.standard`, and the hole states no `standard` that restates it. A size bound by expression binds a `Text` parameter holding the size designation (FreeCAD `ThreadSize`).
- `thread` is the hole's internal thread. For a Fusion Hole with a child Thread, `Bore.diameter` keeps the stored hole diameter when present. An absent hole diameter can use the thread minor diameter with a loss that names the substitution. A thread the source keeps inside the hole record, or as a child record with no feature node of its own (the Fusion Thread scope bound to a hole), is `Hole.thread`; the child record is its native record. A child thread that is a feature node of its own, with a name and a suppression state (the SolidWorks Hole Wizard cosmetic thread, `moDerivedCosmeticThread_c`), is a `Thread` feature whose `face` picks the hole's bore and which follows the hole in feature order. A writer to a format that keeps threads inside the hole may fold such a `Thread` into the hole, charging the loss of its identity.
- `targets` names the bodies the hole cuts (§6); an assembly hole states them by its participants, with `targets: None` (§6.7).
- `series` runs one hole through several parts of an assembly: the hole's definition states `assembly` (§6.7), whose `participants` are the parts it may cut. Each stage names the parts its `parts` picks, each a participant. A `Stated` stage cuts them with its own `shape`, `extent`, `standard`, and `thread`: its `extent` limits the cut in each part it picks, and an `Amount` runs from the first face the stage's axis meets in that part. A `PartFeature` stage is a `Hole` feature of the picked part's own history, which the part opened alone has, placed by the series' positions; the series names it and cuts nothing for it. The hole's own `shape`, `extent`, `standard`, and `thread` cut every participant the axis passes through that no stage picks. An empty `series` is a single hole. SolidWorks stores a series as a hole in each part, grouped and placed by the assembly. The assembly's record holds the series' name, a sketch of the positions, and holders that update the sketch and the hole feature in each cut part, and no size, depth, end condition, or thread; each stage is a complete Hole Wizard feature in its part's own file. So the SolidWorks decoder states one `PartFeature` stage per cut part. No stored file known to the project settles where a SolidWorks blind stage's depth runs from, or what a middle part's size follows (part 11). SolidWorks' Middle Parts automatic size ("Sets the diameter for the middle parts by choosing the closest available hole size to the diameter of the first part") is outside the type: a decoder that meets it keeps the link as the native option `sldprt:hole_series_auto_size`, and a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the feature where it is set. CATIA's series is a stage per series, each picking its parts with a complete hole, and the default hole the hole's own fields, typed from Dassault's page Using Hole Series as `Stated` stages; where a CATIA blind stage's depth runs from is not stated, so a CATIA blind stage states `extent: None` and keeps its depth as a native option (part 11). No stored file known to the project holds a CATIA series, so the CATIA decoder keeps a series as the native option `catia:hole_series` and states `series` empty (typed, carrier unread; part 11). A writer whose target's series is an assembly-level cut writes a `PartFeature` stage as a `Stated` stage from the part hole's `shape`, `extent`, `standard`, and `thread`. A writer whose target has no hole series writes each `Stated` stage as a hole on its parts, a `PartFeature` stage's hole being in its part already, and charges a loss naming the feature.

#### Thread

```rust
pub struct Thread { pub face: SetSelection, pub start: Option<SetSelection>, pub spec: ThreadSpec, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub struct ThreadSpec {
    pub standard: Option<StandardSize>,
    pub major_diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>,
    pub minor_diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>,
    pub pitch_diameter: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>,
    pub pitch: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>>,
    pub hand: Option<Hand>,
    pub length: Option<ThreadLength>,
    pub modeled: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
}
pub enum ThreadLength {
    Full,
    Blind(Dimension<PositiveLength>),
    ToElement { element: SetSelection, offset: Option<Dimension<Length>> },
    Standard,
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
```

- `Thread` threads a cylindrical face that no hole owns: a shaft, a boss, or a bore made by another feature (CATIA thread and tap; Creo, SolidWorks, Fusion, and NX cosmetic and detailed threads). `start` selects the edge or face the thread starts from. A source cosmetic thread that belongs to no hole, or that is a feature node of its own under a hole (above), is a `Thread`.
- `modeled` states whether the body holds the helical form (NX detailed thread, FreeCAD `ModelThread`, SolidWorks thread feature) or carries the thread as data. Fusion stores it in byte 21 after the family string of the `Thread` scope: 1 is `Some(true)`, where the thread's state inserts the helical flank faces, and 0 `Some(false)`, where it only replaces the cylinder's surface.
- `Full` runs over the whole face or hole depth, `Standard` takes the length from the standard's tapped-hole rule, and `ToElement` runs to a limit face or plane (CATIA `ThdBottomLimit`). For a thread, `StandardSize` holds the standard, the size designation, and the tolerance class.

#### Emboss

```rust
pub struct Emboss {
    pub profile: ProfileRef,
    pub effect: EmbossEffect,
    pub face: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub mapping: Option<EmbossMapping>,
    pub direction: Option<Construction<Direction>>,
    pub targets: Option<Targets>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum EmbossEffect {
    Emboss { depth: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>> },
    Engrave { depth: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>> },
    Scribe,
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum EmbossMapping { Wrap, Project, Native(NonBlankString) }
```

- `Emboss` raises (`Emboss`) or sinks (`Engrave`) a profile, often text, by a depth, or imprints it (`Scribe`). `Wrap` maps the profile onto `face` by arc length; `Project` projects it along `direction` (Inventor emboss and engrave, Fusion emboss, SolidWorks wrap). A wrap is an emboss with `Wrap` mapping. `targets` names the bodies the emboss joins or cuts (§6). Fusion states the effect by the sign of its depth; a Fusion emboss whose stored depth is 0 or absent does not state whether it raises or sinks its profile, so it is `EmbossEffect::Native("f3d:wrap_unresolved")` with the stored depth as the native option `f3d:wrap_depth` (typed, carrier unread; part 11).

#### Dome

```rust
pub struct Dome {
    pub faces: SetSelection,
    pub height: Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>>,
    pub concave: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub shape: Option<DomeShape>,
    pub direction: Option<Construction<Direction>>,
    pub points: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum DomeShape { Default, Elliptical, Continuous }
```

- A dome raises each face of `faces` to a smooth cap that meets the face's outline (SolidWorks dome). `height` is the height of the cap's highest point above the face's plane, along the face normal, or along `direction` where it is stated. `concave` makes the cap a recess. `points` constrains the cap by points or a sketch, and then `height` is `None`. On a cylindrical or conical model a `height` of 0 makes the cap tangent to the adjacent face (SolidWorks Dome help and API `IDomeFeatureData2`).
- `shape` states the cap's form: `Elliptical` is a half ellipsoid whose height is one of its radii, on a cylindrical or conical model; `Continuous` slopes up evenly on all sides of a polygonal face, where `Default` rises normal to the polygon's edges (the Dome help). The cap surface is the source's own construction: over a face whose outline is not a circle, SolidWorks builds a degree-5 B-spline that is no sphere and no radial profile from the peak, and near-separable in its own parameters. That surface is the dome's evaluation (K2), as a smoothed curve's is (§6.6). No stored file known to the project settles the surface over a circular face and in the elliptical and continuous forms, and SolidWorks' concave, elliptical, and continuous flags are typed, carrier unread: the record's flag bytes are not framed (part 11).
- A writer whose target has no dome writes the state after the feature as stored geometry (§3.4 step 3): no target builds SolidWorks' fitted cap, so a target's own dome of the same height over the same faces is another surface.

#### Decal

```rust
pub struct Decal {
    pub image: AssetId,
    pub faces: OrderedSelection,
    pub chain_faces: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub opacity: Option<Dimension<Fraction>>,
    pub placement: Option<DecalPlacement>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub struct DecalPlacement {
    pub frame: Construction<Frame>,
    pub width: Dimension<PositiveLength>,
    pub height: Dimension<PositiveLength>,
    pub mirrored: bool,
}
```

- A decal binds a raster image, an `Asset` of the model (§8), to model faces as an appearance: it changes no geometry, so it is stateless (§5.4). The first of `faces` positions and orients the image, and `chain_faces` wraps it onto the faces connected to the first; `opacity` runs from 0, transparent, to 1, opaque (Fusion decal, API `DecalInput`). `chain_faces` and `opacity` are typed from the vendor's description, and a Fusion decoder states neither (part 11). The decal record's one f32, in the domain of an opacity, and its first flag byte are not settled against the decal's appearance or picked faces, so both stay native options of the decal.
- `placement` places the image: `frame` has its origin at the image's centre on the faces, its x axis along the image's width, from left to right, its y axis along its height, from bottom to top, and its z axis, x × y, along the faces' outward normal at the origin, so that x and y span their tangent plane there; `width` and `height` are the image's extents on the faces; `mirrored` reflects the image across its height axis, so its width runs against x. The image lies on the faces by distance from its centre: the image point at distance r from the image's centre, in the direction at angle θ from the width axis toward the height axis, shows at the point of the faces at surface distance r from the origin along the geodesic that leaves the origin at angle θ from x toward y, across face boundaries and onto faces at any angle to z, at the one scale `width` and `height` state. On planes, cylinders, and cones that keeps every length of the image; on a doubly curved face it keeps lengths along the geodesics from the origin and not across them. Where two such geodesics reach one point of the faces the placement does not say which image point shows, and the picture there is the target's. A placement has no other mapping: a source decal whose image lies on its faces another way states no `placement` and keeps its own in its native options.
- Fusion stores the placement in the decal's own record (type `9A9B75AF`, which the Decal scope references), beside a texture coordinate for each vertex of the target body's display mesh: a centre O, two f32 vectors U and V, a unit normal N = U × V / |U × V|, and three flag bytes. The texture coordinates put (0.5, 0.5) at O, u increasing along U and v along −V; and the length per unit u on faces facing N is √2·|U|·pw/m, per unit v √2·|V|·ph/m, for an image of pw × ph pixels with m the larger. So `frame` is O with x along U, y along V, and z along N, and `width` and `height` are √2·|U|·pw/m and √2·|V|·ph/m. That N is the faces' outward normal at O is inferred from the decal's lying on them: N = U × V, and O lies on the mesh. That y runs toward the image's top, so that texture v runs from its top row, is inferred from the unmirrored decals' frames being right-handed with N (part 11).
- Two of the flag bytes reverse an axis of the image. The second is the mirror: where it is 1, u runs along −U. The third reverses the height: where it is 1, v runs along +V, where at 0 it runs along −V. The frame holds both with the one flag, since an image reversed along its height is the image mirrored and turned half a turn about z: where the third byte is 1 the decoder states x along −U and y along −V, and `mirrored` is true where exactly one of the two bytes is 1. A second flag would state each picture twice. Both readings are thin (part 11).
- A Fusion decal stores the coordinates of that one mapping, computed on the body's display mesh, and no stored value selects another. No decal is a projection along N: on the plane through O the stored coordinates equal the projection, and off it they do not. On a cylinder the stored coordinates keep length both along the geodesics from O and across them; on doubly curved faces they keep it along and not across. Some mesh edges tilted to N have their projected length in place of their length in the image, on walls that stand perpendicular to the decal's plane, and no field of the decal record or of the records it references tells them apart; that this collapse comes from the display mesh, where a vertex shared across a sharp edge carries the normal of one of its faces and a step along that normal has no length in the vertex's tangent plane, is inferred. The collapse belongs to one tessellation and is no part of the placement. So the decoder states the `placement` of every Fusion decal from the record, not from the coordinates; it keeps the per-vertex coordinates with their triangle list and mesh reference, a cache of the mapping on one tessellation, and the record's two unplaced f64 values, its f32, and its first flag byte, as native options of the decal, which a Fusion writer writes back. A writer whose target has decals writes the image, faces, opacity, and placement, and charges a loss naming the feature where its target's decal lays the image another way; a target with no decal charges a loss naming the feature.

### 6.5 Patterns, template instances, and body operations

#### Patterns and mirrors

A pattern repeats seeds along a layout. A mirror is a pattern whose layout is one reflection. Component patterns and mirrors are assembly operations (§6.7) and reuse the layouts below.

```rust
pub struct Pattern {
    pub seeds: PatternSeeds,
    pub layout: PatternLayout,
    pub instances: PatternInstances,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum PatternSeeds {
    Features { features: OrderedSelection, method: Option<PatternMethod> },
    Faces(SetSelection),
    Bodies { bodies: SetSelection, join: Option<bool> },
}
pub enum PatternMethod { Identical, Adjust { against: Option<AdjustAgainst> }, Native(NonBlankString) }
pub enum AdjustAgainst { ModelSoFar, ModelBefore }

pub enum PatternLayout {
    Linear(LinearLayout),
    Circular(CircularLayout),
    Path       { path: PathRef, run: PatternRun<Length>, orientation: Option<InstanceOrientation> },
    Points     { points: OrderedSelection, reference: Option<Locus> },
    Dimensions(Vec<DimensionRun>),
    Table(DimensionTable),
    Mirror(MirrorLayout),
    Composite(Vec<CompositeStage>),
    Scale(ScaleLayout),
    Follow(OrderedSelection),
    Chain(ChainLayout),
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum CompositeStage {
    Linear(LinearLayout),
    Circular(CircularLayout),
    Mirror(MirrorLayout),
    Scale(ScaleLayout),
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub struct LinearLayout { pub first: LinearRun, pub second: Option<LinearRun>, pub seed_only: Option<Dimension<bool>> }
pub struct CircularLayout {
    pub axis: Construction<Axis>, pub angular: PatternRun<Angle>, pub radial: Option<PatternRun<Length>>,
    pub orientation: Option<InstanceOrientation>,
}
pub struct MirrorLayout { pub plane: Construction<Plane>, pub stitch_tolerance: Option<Dimension<Length>> }
pub struct ScaleLayout { pub factor: Dimension<PositiveReal>, pub count: Dimension<u32>, pub center: Locus }
pub struct ChainLayout { pub path: PathRef, pub links: ChainLinks }
pub enum ChainLinks { Connected(Vec<ChainLink>), Native { kind: NonBlankString, picks: OrderedSelection } }
pub struct ChainLink { pub pins: [Construction<Axis>; 2] }
pub struct LinearRun { pub direction: Construction<Direction>, pub run: PatternRun<Length> }
pub struct PatternRun<Q> {
    pub spacing: Spacing<Q>,
    pub sides: Option<RunSides<Q>>,
    pub seed: Option<Dimension<u32>>,
    pub increments: Vec<Increment>,
}
pub enum RunSides<Q> {
    One,
    Against,
    Symmetric { count: Option<SymmetricMeasure>, extent: Option<SymmetricMeasure> },
    Reverse(Spacing<Q>),
}
pub enum Spacing<Q> {
    Pitch     { count: Dimension<u32>, pitch: Dimension<Q> },
    Span      { count: Dimension<u32>, span: Dimension<Q> },
    PitchSpan { pitch: Dimension<Q>, span: Dimension<Q> },
    Fit       { count: Dimension<u32> },
    UpTo      { reference: OrderedSelection, fill: UpToFill<Q>, offset: Option<Dimension<Q>>, from: Option<Locus> },
    List(Vec<Dimension<Q>>),
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum UpToFill<Q> { Count(Dimension<u32>), Pitch(Dimension<Q>) }
pub enum Locus { Centroid, Point(Construction<Point>) }
pub enum InstanceOrientation {
    Fixed, Follow, Frenet,
    Rolled { reference: PathReference, reference_axis: FrameAxis, seed_axis: Option<Construction<Direction>> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum PathReference { PlaneNormal, Direction(Construction<Direction>) }
pub struct Increment { pub parameter: ParameterId, pub step: ScalarDimension }
pub struct DimensionRun { pub count: Dimension<u32>, pub increments: Vec<Increment> }
pub struct DimensionTable { pub parameters: Vec<ParameterId>, pub rows: Vec<TableRow> }
pub struct TableRow { pub instance: u32, pub values: Vec<Option<ScalarDimension>> }

pub enum PatternInstances {
    Implicit(Vec<InstanceOverride>),
    Members(Vec<PatternMember>),
}
pub struct InstanceIndex(pub Vec<i32>);
pub struct InstanceOverride { pub index: InstanceIndex, pub change: InstanceChange }
pub enum InstanceChange { Skipped, Varied { parameters: BTreeMap<ParameterId, Expression> } }
pub struct PatternMember { pub index: InstanceIndex, pub features: Vec<FeatureId> }
```

**What is patterned.**
- `Features` repeats the seed features: each pick is `FeatureResult(f)`, in source order. Each instance applies the seed features' definitions at the instance's placement. `method` states how: `Identical` copies the seed's result, its intersections with the model included, to each instance (SolidWorks geometry pattern, Fusion identical compute); `Adjust` builds each instance at its placement and solves its terminations and intersections against the model. `against` states which model: `ModelSoFar`, the model as the instances before it left it, each instance built and intersected in turn; `ModelBefore`, the model as it stood before the pattern, every instance built against it and all of them intersected with it at once, so a termination such as up to next resolves once for the group; `None` does not state which (Fusion adjust, Inventor's patterns, and NX variational, on which no stored file known to the project settles it, part 11). Inventor stores one compute code (0) on every pattern and mirror, so no stored value separates identical from adjust. Where the copies of an Inventor feature pattern differ from the seed, each copy the seed's feature intersected with the model at its own place, `Identical` cannot give them; where a seed ends on the model (up to next, to, through all), that does not separate `Adjust` from a third construction, the seed's terminations kept and the intersections solved at each copy. So the Inventor decoder states `Adjust { against: None }` only where the copies differ from the seed and every seed's extents are distances, where the two readings give one solid, and otherwise `method: None` with the code kept as the native option `inventor:pattern_compute` (Rule N case (a), part 11). Where no two instances meet and no instance's termination depends on another instance, the two give one result. Creo's identical, general, and variable regenerations are `Identical`, `Adjust` against `ModelSoFar`, and `Adjust` against `ModelBefore` (PTC About Pattern Regeneration Options). The vendor states as a requirement of the variable option that no instance intersects another ("No instance intersects any other instance"), and states that the system does not check its requirements for the identical option only; of the variable option the page gives the construction and no failure, so an instance set that breaks the requirement gives another result than a general pattern's. Creo stores the choice as one of the `pat_type` bits 4, 8, and 32, exactly one of which is set, repeated in every member's `create_status`, and each bit is read by which record holds the edges where the instances meet the part: under bit 32 every member holds copies of the leader's intersection edges and none of its own, which is `Identical`; under bit 8 the leader holds the intersection edges of every instance and the members hold none, which is `ModelBefore`; under bit 4 members hold intersection edges of their own (the G form), which is `ModelSoFar`. A writer writes the target's adjusting pattern and charges a loss naming the feature unless one of two things holds: `against` is stated and is the construction the target's format is established to use, or the writer establishes on the evaluated instances that no two of them meet and that no instance's termination resolves on geometry another instance made, which is where the two constructions give one result. Two instances meet when an edge of the evaluated result joins a face of one to a face of another. `None` is neither construction, so the rule is one rule in both directions, and a source that does not state which is charged like a source that states the other. The construction is established for Creo's general and variable options and inferred for CATIA keep specifications (below), so a writer to CATIA is free of the loss by the first test where `against` is `ModelSoFar`. Which one the adjusting pattern of Fusion, Inventor, or NX uses, no stored file known to the project settles. CATIA keep specifications is `Adjust { against: Some(ModelSoFar) }`. Its carrier is the pattern's `DesignIntent` 2, and that 2 means keep specifications is inferred, by elimination of the dialog's other options, which have fields of their own; `DesignIntent` 1 is `Identical` (inferred). A pattern that stores per-instance copies of the seed stores each instance's result solid with the body's objects after that step, every step after the first keeping cells earlier instances made, which `ModelBefore` cannot give: `ModelSoFar` is inferred from that stored build order; a pattern that stores one pattern-level result holds no build order, and its construction is inferred from the option. The construction falls under Rule H1: the CATIA decoder states `against: Some(ModelSoFar)` where the pattern stores its build and the build agrees, and `against: None` otherwise. So a writer of Fusion, Inventor, or NX is free of the loss by the second test only. Bits 1 and 2 of Creo's `pat_type` count the directions that hold more than one instance, and bit 256 marks a reference pattern, whose layout is another pattern's. A pattern of a group or template instance picks the result of each grouped feature or of the instance. SolidWorks' propagate visual properties is an option of its patterns, which says whether the instances take the seed's colours and textures (the vendor's API has it on pattern feature data and says only true or false). A stored part needs no field for it: each instance face that carries a seed's colour stores that colour as its own, so a reader reproduces the stored part from the faces. Its carrier narrows to two bytes of the pattern's option block, the block located from its end through the sub-objects nested in the record. No stored file known to the project settles which byte is the option, nor whether either byte says that the instances take the seed's colour. So it is the pattern's native option `sldprt:propagate_visual_properties`, with both bytes kept (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- `Faces` copies the seed faces into their body at each instance (SolidWorks, Fusion, and NX face patterns).
- `Bodies` copies whole bodies as new bodies. `join` merges each copy with its seed: SolidWorks merge solids and knit surfaces, FreeCAD Draft array `Fuse`, a CATIA pattern of the current solid. A reflected copy of bodies (FreeCAD `Part::Mirroring`, SolidWorks body mirror) is a `Bodies` pattern with a `Mirror` layout.

**Layouts.** Every direction, axis, and plane is a `Construction` (§5.9): a pattern direction along an edge or sketch axis, a circular axis through a cylinder or a sketch normal, a mirror plane on a datum or a planar face. A feature-private plane or axis (Inventor mirror planes and circular axes) is the operand's inline construction. A reversed direction is a `Flip` step of the construction. A frozen axis or plane with no reference (Fusion inline axes) is a construction with no inputs and a resolved value.
- `Linear` (`LinearLayout`) holds one or two runs, each along its own direction. `seed_only` states that the second run repeats only the seed, not the first run's instances (SolidWorks pattern seed only; NX `SeedOnlyToggle`): the instances that then exist are `[i, 0]` and `[0, j]`. An implicit pattern stores its two counts and not that index set, so `seed_only` is the only record of which instances exist. It occurs only with a `second` run.
- `Circular` (`CircularLayout`) holds an angular run about `axis` and an optional radial run outward from it (CATIA crowns). SolidWorks circular Direction 2 is the angular run's reverse side (`sides`), not a second angular run.
- `Path` places instances along a path (SolidWorks curve pattern, Fusion path pattern, FreeCAD path array, NX along path), `run` stating their spacing by arc length. A Fusion path pattern's count with its spacing between neighbours is `Pitch`, and with its extent from the first instance to the last `Span`; where the decoder does not read the count or the distance, the run's spacing is `Spacing::Native("f3d:path_spacing")` with the values it reads as native options (typed, carrier unread; part 11). Its flip runs the instances against the path's direction (`RunSides::Against`). A settings record of the reordered form is read at the offsets of the 267-byte form on an assumption, so for it the decoder states the spacing `Spacing::Native("f3d:path_spacing")`, `sides: None`, and `orientation: None`, with the count, the distance, and the distance-type, flip, and orientation bytes as native options (Rule N case (a), part 11). A seed member of role `0x4` is read as a feature on an assumption, so the decoder states it as a `Native` pick with its stored identity (Rule N case (a), part 11). Its start, a parameter of the path curve stored with two of the start point's coordinates, is the native option `f3d:path_start` (Rule N case (a), part 11): a `Path` run starts at the seed.
- `Points` places one instance at each picked point (sketch points, vertices, datum points), in pick order; `reference` is the point of the seed that lands on each (CATIA anchor point; SolidWorks centroid or selected point). NX's general pattern with point locations is `Points` with `reference: Some(Point(..))`: its pattern definition stores the from-point, and each instance's placement matrix the translation that carries it to the instance's to-point (part 11).
- `Dimensions` is Creo's dimension pattern. Each run has a count and the seed dimensions it increments; the instance placement follows from the incremented placement dimensions, so there is no direction. `Table` is Creo's table pattern: one row per instance, with a value per table dimension, `None` where the row keeps the seed's value.
- `Mirror` (`MirrorLayout`) reflects the seeds across `plane`. Its one instance is the reflection. `stitch_tolerance` is the tolerance with which the mirror stitches the reflection to its seed, whatever the seeds are (Fusion `mirrorStitchTolerance`).
- `Composite` applies its stages in order, each to every instance the earlier stages produced (FreeCAD MultiTransform), except that a `Scale` stage after the first does not multiply them: it splits the instances made so far into `count` consecutive slices of equal length and scales every instance of slice j by slice j's factor about that instance's own transformed centre, and its coordinate is the slice (`PartDesign/App/FeatureMultiTransform.cpp` at 1.1.4). A stage is a linear, circular, or mirror layout or a scale, the four transformations FreeCAD's MultiTransform dialog adds (`LinearPattern`, `PolarPattern`, `Mirrored`, and `Scaled`; `PartDesign/Gui/TaskMultiTransformParameters.cpp` at 1.1.4), and holds the same struct as the layout of that name, with the same meaning. A MultiTransform with one transformation is that transformation's layout. FreeCAD also computes a MultiTransform that lists another among its transformations, which the dialog does not make and no stored file known to the project holds. The inner one is a `CompositeStage::Native` stage. `CompositeStage::Native` keeps that stage, and a stage of a class whose meaning is not established (Rule N case (a), part 11), named `fcstd:<class>`. Its properties are native options of the pattern, each keyed by the stage's source object and the property (`fcstd:<object>.<property>`), so two such stages share no key. A composite that holds one states no coordinate count for it.
- `Scale` (`ScaleLayout`) makes `count` instances, the seed included: instance i, for i from 0 to count − 1, is the seed scaled uniformly by 1 + i (factor − 1)/(count − 1) about `center`, so the last is scaled by `factor`. `Centroid` is the volume centroid of the first seed feature's tool solid, the solid it adds or removes (FreeCAD PartDesign `Scaled`: `PartDesign/App/FeatureScaled.cpp` at 1.1.4). A `Scaled` in whole-shape mode, which has no original, scales the whole solid entering it: it is a `Bodies` pattern of that solid with `join: Some(true)`, whose `center` is the origin of the base feature's placement in body coordinates, a `Point` construction at `Coordinates` (0, 0, 0) of a `Built` copy of that feature's `placement` (§5.10), and its result takes the base feature's placement; a sketch-based feature carries its predecessor's placement, and a body's first `Pad` the body origin (`FeatureScaled.cpp`, `FeatureTransformed.cpp`). A writer whose target has no scaled pattern cannot copy the instances as bodies: a seed that adds to or cuts a body leaves no body of its own, and `Centroid` is the centroid of a tool solid that no state the document holds as a body. It writes, per instance after the seed, the seed feature's definition again as a new body, a uniform scale of that body about its own centroid by the instance's factor, and a combine with the seed's Boolean, three geometry features each, which §3.4's rules for a construction govern, and charges `export:feature.lowered`; this holds only where the pattern has one seed feature, the target can write that feature as a new body, and the target's scale takes a body's centroid as its centre, and otherwise step 3 applies.
- `Follow` takes its instance set and indices from another pattern, which its one pick names (a `FeatureResult` pick of a pattern feature; in an assembly, of a part pattern through an occurrence context, or of a component pattern): it makes one instance per instance index of that pattern other than the seed's, with that index, and instance k is the seeds rebuilt with every reference to geometry of the followed pattern's seed result replaced by the same geometry of its instance k, so a placement that rests only on the followed seed moves with that instance, and a part of the placement held by another reference stays. Creo's reference pattern (`pat_type` bit 256, `pat_feat_id` naming the followed pattern's leader) is `Follow` where `pat_feat_id` names a pattern leader of the same model: its member index tuples are the followed pattern's, and it stores no increment. A header that names no pattern leader is `Native("creo:reference_pattern")`. A component pattern that follows a pattern (CATIA Reuse Pattern, a SolidWorks pattern-driven pattern) is `Follow` (§6.7). A writer whose target has no such pattern writes the instances as members (`PatternInstances::Members`, or placed occurrences for a component pattern) and charges a loss naming the pattern.
- `Chain` places components along `path`, a path that lies in one plane, each instance keeping the seed's relation to that plane; it occurs only in a component pattern (§6.7). `Connected` takes the seeds in turn, one `ChainLink` per seed in the order the seeds alternate, its `pins` two axes of that seed's own geometry: each link's first pin axis is the previous link's second, both pin axes of every link lie on the path, and consecutive pin axes are therefore a chord of the path as long as the link's own pin distance. `ChainLinks::Native` keeps a linkage whose meaning is not established (Rule N case (a), part 11), `kind` naming the source's form and `picks` the entities of the seeds it picks, with its values as the pattern's native options: a writer of the source's format writes it back and a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the pattern. SolidWorks' chain pattern (`moLocalChainPattern_c`): its connected linkage is `Connected`; its data object's words are its seeds' transform stamps, one per seed, so the decoder joins seeds by stamp and takes each seed's pins from its geometry, since the path-link references of the record's inputs list are not read (typed, carrier unread; part 11); its `D1` and `D2` stay native options. Its distance form is `ChainLinks::Native` with `kind` `sldprt:distance_chain`, its path link the picks and its spacing, measure, orientation, and count native options: no stored file known to the project holds a distance chain, and SolidWorks' Chain Pattern PropertyManager pages name the path link ("Select a cylindrical face, circular edge, linear edge, sketch point, vertex, or reference axis"), the spacing, and the alignment ("Distance along path", "Linear distance", "Tangent to curve", "Align to seed") without saying where the link is held on the path or between which points the spacing runs, so they do not define the result (part 11). Its distance linkage, which takes two path links ("Path Link 1", "Path Link 2") and whose spacing points the pages leave open, is `PatternLayout::Native`, as is a chain on a path that is not planar (part 11). A writer whose target has no chain pattern writes the instances as placed occurrences and charges a loss naming the pattern.
- `Native` keeps a layout whose meaning is not established (Rule N case (a), part 11): NX polygon, spiral, helix, fill, and feature reference layouts, an NX general pattern whose locations are coordinate systems, and coordinate tables, none of which any stored file known to the project uses; and a Creo reference pattern that names no pattern leader. Its parameters go to `native_options` under their source names (`nx:<name>`, `fcstd:<name>`).
- NX's pattern frame only (`FrameOnlyToggle`, a dialog name that no file stores) is the native option `nx:frame_only`, and its clocking, which NX stores on one instance and not on the pattern, is the native option `nx:clocking` of that instance, its four expressions and its integer kept (Rule N case (a), part 11). The pattern record is a run of sub-objects, each introduced by its class selector, and each instance row a 4 × 4 placement matrix that the decoder joins to stored faces. A rectangular record that runs in two directions, every translation i·a + j·b for two vectors, says so in one byte of the layout run, ahead of `PatternFill`: 1 for two directions, 0 for one line. Byte 1 is `LinearLayout.second` with the second `DistancePatternSpacing` as its `Spacing::Pitch`, and byte 0 is `second: None` with the stored second spacing kept in `source_settings`. No stored file known to the project settles frame only or clocking. Siemens' NX pages are behind a login. NX's along-path layout (`AlongPathPattern`) is `Path`. Its direction-1 `OnPathDistancePatternSpacing` of type `00 02` holds the instance count and, in its third expression, a value that reads as a percent of the path's length; its second expression, the pitch of the other spacing types, stays a native option, and the direction-2 run and the `DistancePatternSpacing` need no field. At 100 % the instances, seed included, run evenly over the whole of the path, which is `run` with `Spacing::Fit { count }`. That reading is under Rule H1: the NX decoder states `Fit` only where the stored percent is 100 and the stored instance matrices lie evenly over the whole path, and `PatternLayout::Native("nx:along_path")` otherwise; a run over a share of the path is open (part 11). Frame only decides which instances exist, so a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the feature. An NX circular pattern's `orientation` is read from its instance matrices: a matrix that rotates the seed about the axis by its angular step is `Follow`, and a matrix with the identity rotation on a circular layout is `Fixed`; linear and general instances are translations. The `PatternOrientation` byte, 06 on circular records and 01 on linear and general ones, co-varies with the layout, and the value a circular pattern of `Fixed` instances stores is not read (typed, carrier unread; part 11), so an NX writer keeps the byte as the native option `nx:pattern_orientation`. NX's single output is the form of `instances`: the record's child list names one `Instance Feature` per instance (kind 03), which is `PatternInstances::Members`, each member's `features` its `Instance Feature` in child-ordinal order, or one `Multi Instance Output` feature that applies every instance and writes one body (kind 02), which is `Implicit`; the geometry is the same in both forms. The record-level value that stores the option (the lane count) is open (part 11), so it stays the native option `nx:single_output` for an NX writer, and a writer whose target has only one of the two forms writes the other with a loss naming the feature.

**Runs and spacing.**
- Every count includes the seed.
- `Pitch` is count and spacing between neighbours. `Span` is count and the distance or angle from the first instance to the last. `PitchSpan` is spacing and total extent, with the count derived (CATIA spacing and length, NX pitch and span). `List` holds the spacing between each neighbour pair, in order, so the count is its length plus one (CATIA unequal spacing, FreeCAD `Spacings`, NX list).
- An angular `Span` of a full turn spaces the instances periodically: the last instance does not repeat the first. Any other span places the first and last instance at its ends.
- `Fit` spreads `count` instances over the whole path or the whole turn (CATIA complete crown, FreeCAD path array, Inventor fit to path).
- `UpTo` fills a linear run up to `reference`, measured from `from` on the seed and stopping `offset` short of the reference, with either a count or a spacing (SolidWorks up to reference).
- `sides` states where the run places its instances. `One` places them along the run's direction from the seed. `Against` places them against the run's direction from the seed, so their coordinates are negative; it occurs only in a `Path` run, whose direction is the path's own, from its first pick to its last in path order, and on a path of one pick that curve's own direction (Fusion's path pattern flip). `Symmetric` mirrors the run onto the reverse side: `count: Some(PerSide)` counts each side's instances with the seed in each (SolidWorks circular symmetric: 2n − 1 in all), `Some(Total)` counts every instance, and `extent` states the same choice for the distance of a `Span` or `PitchSpan`. `None` in either means not read, and since each decides how the stored count or distance is read, a writer of another codec does not write that number and charges a loss naming the pattern (§2.4). `Total` with n instances puts ⌊(n−1)/2⌋ on the reverse side and ⌈(n−1)/2⌉ along the direction, so the unpaired instance of an even count lies on the positive side. Fusion's symmetric count is `Total`, on sketch and on feature rectangular patterns. A Fusion feature pattern's symmetric extent is `PerSide`, the distance from the seed to the last instance on one side, and the byte after the `ffffffff` sentinel of the scope's first referenced record (type `EA0E146E`) states whether the stored distance is the run's `Span` (1) or its `Pitch` (0). No stored file known to the project settles a Fusion sketch pattern's symmetric extent, so it states `extent: None`. Fusion stores a sketch pattern's symmetry in the second and third flags of the pattern's class prefix, direction one and direction two, and its instances in the order seed, reverse side far to near, forward side near to far, which the index does not follow (Instances, below). A Fusion feature pattern's payload states each direction's sides in the direction's symmetric byte, and the run's `sides` follows it: `Symmetric` where the byte states a symmetric direction that places instances, `One` where it does not; no stored file known to the project settles circular symmetric patterns (part 11). `Reverse` is a second arm against the run's direction with its own spacing (SolidWorks circular Direction 2 with symmetric cleared). `sides: None` states nothing.
- `seed` is the seed's step count from the run's first instance (CATIA `Posi`, `Posj`): the run's instances then span coordinates −`seed` to count − 1 − `seed`. `None` places the seed first.
- **Coordinate range.** A run's count is the count its spacing states, the seed included: the `count` of `Pitch`, `Span`, `Fit`, and `UpTo` with `Count`, and the length of a `List` plus one. `PitchSpan`, `UpTo` with `Pitch`, and `Native` state none. Where that count is literal, n, with `last` = n − 1, and `seed` is `None` (s = 0) or literal (s), the run's coordinates are: under `One`, −s to `last` − s; under `Against`, s − `last` to s; under `Symmetric` with `count: Some(Total)`, −⌊`last`/2⌋ to `last` − ⌊`last`/2⌋; under any other `Symmetric`, −`last` to `last`; under `Reverse(r)`, from the lesser of 1 − m and −s to `last` − s, where m is r's count, and with no lower bound where r states no literal count; and under `sides: None`, at most `last` with no lower bound, since an unread side may be a `Reverse` arm, whose count the run does not state. A run with no literal count has no range, and neither has one whose `seed` is a parameter under an arm whose range reads s. A `Dimensions` run of literal count n has coordinates 0 to n − 1. Part 10 checks an instance index against these ranges.
- `increments` change listed parameters of the seed definition by `step` per coordinate along the run (Creo dimension increments; SolidWorks and NX varied instances). The increment is a dimension, so a parameter can drive it.
- `orientation` states whether a circular or path instance keeps the seed's orientation (`Fixed`), turns with the layout (`Follow`: about the axis, or tangent to the path), or follows the path's Frenet frame (`Frenet`). `Rolled` puts the instance's x axis on the path tangent and its `reference_axis`, `Y` or `Z`, on the `reference` direction made orthogonal to the tangent, the third axis completing a right-handed frame, after turning the seed so that its `seed_axis`, or its x axis where that is `None`, lies on its x axis; `PlaneNormal` is the normal of the path's plane on the side of the z axis of the path's placement, and the definition's +Z for a path that is not planar. A FreeCAD Draft `PathArray` aligned `Frenet` is `Frenet`, and one with `Align` false `Fixed`; its `Original` mode is `Rolled { reference: PlaneNormal, reference_axis: Y, seed_axis: None }`, with `ForceVertical` `Rolled { reference: Direction(VerticalVector), reference_axis: Z, .. }`, and its `Tangent` mode sets `seed_axis` to its `TangentVector` (`patharray.py` `placements_on_path`, `calculate_placement`, and `get_shape_normal`). A writer whose target's path pattern takes no such roll writes `Follow` and charges a loss naming the pattern.

**Instances.** An instance is named by its `InstanceIndex`: one coordinate per run present, in declaration order; a missing optional run contributes no coordinate. A run the source stores is present whatever its count: a Fusion rectangular pattern stores both directions, so its second direction with quantity 1 is a `second` run, and its instances are `[i, 0]`. A run the source stores as off is absent (§2.4). `Linear` gives `[first, second]`, or `[first]` with no `second`; `Circular` gives `[angular, radial]`, or `[angular]` with no `radial`; `Dimensions` one per run, `Path`, `Points`, `Table`, and `Mirror` one each, and `Composite` the concatenation of its stages' coordinates. Along a run, a coordinate is the instance's signed step count from the seed along the run's direction, and along an angular run in the direction of positive angle about the axis: the seed is 0 on every run, and the reverse side has negative coordinates, so no source's order of generation enters the index. The instance at `points[k]` has coordinate k + 1. A `Table` instance has its row's `instance`. The mirror image is `[1]`.
- `Implicit` instances exist only as the pattern's result. An override applies to one instance. `Skipped` leaves the instance out, and the other instances keep their coordinates (SolidWorks instances to skip, Inventor per-instance suppression, NX suppression). `Varied` replaces the expression of seed parameters within that instance (SolidWorks and NX varied instances).
- `Members` instances are features of their own (Creo pattern members, NX output as copies of input features). Each member lists one feature per seed feature, in seed order. An index the layout counts and `members` omits is a skipped instance; a member feature that exists and is suppressed is a suppressed member. Where the pattern's container is ordered, the member features follow the pattern contiguously in it. Each member feature holds its own definition, ids, name, and suppression, so the pattern states no override for it, and no member has `driven_by` (§5.10): the pattern's list is the one home of the generation. A member dimension that the pattern increments is the pattern's evaluation (K2): seed value plus coordinate times step.
- A pattern with members adds no geometry of its own and has no evaluation (D35). In an ordered container it sits after its seeds and before its members, and the state after it equals the state before it; in an unordered container it has no result (§5.3).

**Names.** An entity of an implicit instance is named `TopoName::Instance { feature, instance, of }`, where `feature` is the pattern, `instance` the instance index, and `of` the name of the seed entity it copies (§5.7). The seed's own entities keep their unwrapped names. An entity of a member feature is named by that feature (`Generated { feature: member, .. }`) and carries no `Instance` wrapper. Sources map as follows:
- SolidWorks `LPattern(P, i, j, n)` is `[i, j]`, and `[i]` for a one-direction pattern, whose zero `j` stays in the native name; `CirPattern2(P, k, m, n)` is `[k]`, or `[−m]` for a Direction 2 instance; `CurvePattern(P, k, 0, n)` is `[k]`; `MirPattern(M, n)` is `[1]`. The meaning of `i` and `j`, and of `m`, is inferred.
- Inventor prepends `(pattern, code)`. The decoder inverts the pairing `code = (i + j)(i + j + 1)/2 + j` over the source's 1-based indices to zero-based coordinates; the pairing is inferred. Mirror code 2 is `[1]`.
- Fusion allocates one id per instance. The id stays in `NameEntry.native`; the coordinate is derived from creation order, marked `inferred`.
- FreeCAD stores no index. The decoder derives the coordinate from the instance transform by geometry, marked `inferred` (§5.7, derivation).
- A writer stamps instance names only by these rules. Elsewhere it resolves the pick by its witness (§3.4).

**Mapping.** A target without member features receives the pattern as `Implicit`; a member whose definition differs from the seed's beyond the increments is a loss naming the member. A target without `Dimensions` or `Table` receives the instance features as plain features, with a loss naming the pattern. A writer to Creo from an implicit pattern writes members. A target with no second linear direction receives the second run as a loss naming the pattern.

#### Template instances

A template instance is a group of features created from a template, with the template's inputs bound to selections and its parameters to design parameters: a Creo UDF or copied group placed with new references, a CATIA PowerCopy or user feature, an Inventor iFeature.

```rust
pub struct TemplateInstance {
    pub template: Template,
    pub inputs: Vec<TemplateInput>,
    pub parameters: Vec<TemplateParameter>,
    pub members: Vec<FeatureId>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub struct Template {
    pub name: Option<NonBlankString>,
    pub library: Option<ExternalDocument>,
    pub variant: Option<NonBlankString>,
}
pub struct TemplateInput { pub role: Option<NonBlankString>, pub reference: OrderedSelection }
pub struct TemplateParameter { pub role: Option<NonBlankString>, pub parameter: ParameterId }
```

- `template` identifies the template: its name, the library document it came from (§8.1 `ExternalDocument`), and the row of a template family table (Creo UDF family tables).
- `inputs` lists the template's inputs in the template's order, each with the source's role name where it has one and the selection it is bound to. A Creo input's role is its group's `gp_keys` prompt (`new_refs` holds no text); a NULL or empty prompt gives `None`.
- A member operand that the template binds to input `i` picks `PickTarget::TemplateInput { instance, input: i }`, which resolves through the instance's `inputs[i]` in the instance's anchored state. The instance's input is then the one home of that reference: rebinding the input moves every member operand bound to it.
- `parameters` binds each template parameter to a design parameter of the scope. Member dimensions bind that parameter.
- `members` are the features the instance created. Where the instance's container is ordered, they follow the instance contiguously in it, and none has `driven_by`. The instance adds no geometry of its own: in an ordered container the state after it equals the state before it (D35), and in an unordered container it has no result (§5.3). An instance whose source stores no member features has one member: a `Stored` feature (§5.10) that names the instance's result bodies, which the state after it holds. CATIA user-feature instances and Inventor iFeatures store their members as ordinary features, evaluated in order. A CATIA instance holds the template body's features, whose dimensions stored formulas bind to the instance's published parameters, and an `Assemble` that unions that body into the body before the instance; the naming report roots the instance's faces at its member `Groove`, and the faces carry the published diameters. An Inventor iFeature is a record of type `f02ef34e` at the top level of the history that owns a group label whose participants, a sketched feature of class `557fe885` and a chamfer, each name their own faces. The CATIA `UdfBlackBox` flag stays the native option `catia:udf_black_box` (part 11).
- A Creo group without new references is a `Folder` (§5.2), not a template instance.
- A target with templates (Creo, CATIA, Inventor) writes the instance and its bindings. Any other target writes the members as features, with a loss naming the instance.

#### Body operations

```rust
pub struct Combine {
    pub target: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub tools: OrderedSelection,
    pub op: Option<BooleanOp>,
    pub tools_after: Option<ToolDisposition>,
    pub new_component: Option<NewComponent>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum ToolDisposition { Kept, Consumed, Absorbed }
pub struct NewComponent { pub occurrence: OccurrenceId }

pub struct Split { pub mode: SplitMode, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub enum SplitMode {
    ByTools {
        targets: Option<SetSelection>,
        tools: SplitTool,
        method: Option<SplitMethod>,
        kept: Option<Kept<Dimension<bool>>>,
    },
    Mutual {
        elements: OrderedSelection,
        kept: Option<Kept<Vec<Option<Dimension<bool>>>>>,
    },
}
pub enum SplitTool {
    Plane(Construction<Plane>),
    Geometry { tools: SetSelection, extend: Option<ToolExtension> },
    Silhouette(Construction<Direction>),
}
pub enum ToolExtension { Off, Extended { method: Option<ExtendMethod> } }
pub enum SplitMethod { Intersect, Project(ProjectionDirection) }
pub enum Kept<S> {
    All { form: Option<PieceForm> },
    Side { side: S },
    Pieces { keep: Option<SetSelection>, remove: Option<SetSelection> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum PieceForm { Bodies, Regions, Faces }

pub struct DeleteBodies { pub bodies: SetSelection, pub retain: Option<Retention>, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub enum Retention { DeleteSelected, KeepSelected }

pub struct Extract { pub source: SetSelection, pub reversed: Option<bool>, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }

pub struct TransformBodies { pub bodies: SetSelection, pub transformation: Transformation, pub mode: Option<TransformMode>, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub enum TransformMode { Move, Copy { count: Dimension<u32>, divisions: Option<Dimension<u32>> } }
pub struct Transformation { pub steps: Vec<TransformStep>, pub resolved: Option<Transform> }
pub enum TransformStep {
    Translate    { direction: Construction<Direction>, distance: Dimension<Length> },
    Components   { frame: Option<Construction<Frame>>, delta: [Dimension<Length>; 3] },
    PointToPoint { from: Construction<Point>, to: Construction<Point> },
    Rotate       { axis: Construction<Axis>, angle: Dimension<Angle> },
    FrameToFrame { from: Construction<Frame>, to: Construction<Frame> },
    Scale        { center: Option<Locus>, factors: ScaleFactors },
    Fixed(Transform),
    Constrained { mates: Vec<BodyMate> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub struct BodyMate { pub connectors: [JointConnector; 2], pub kind: JointKind, pub alignment: Option<Alignment> }
pub enum ScaleFactors {
    Uniform(Dimension<NonZeroReal>),
    PerAxis { factors: [Dimension<NonZeroReal>; 3], frame: Option<Construction<Frame>> },
}

pub struct MoveFaces { pub faces: SetSelection, pub transformation: Transformation, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub struct DeleteFaces { pub faces: SetSelection, pub heal: Option<Heal>, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub enum Heal { Open, Extend, Fill { tangent: Option<Dimension<bool>> }, Native(NonBlankString) }
pub struct ReplaceFaces { pub faces: SetSelection, pub replacement: SetSelection, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub struct Graft { pub body: SetSelection, pub sheet: SetSelection, pub flip: Option<Dimension<bool>>, pub simplify: Option<Dimension<bool>>, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
```

**Combine.**
- `target` selects the body the result keeps the identity of, anchored `Input`. A CATIA Boolean targets the body it sits in, picked by its `Root` name, and so does a FreeCAD PartDesign Boolean. `None` states that the source names no target: FreeCAD `MultiFuse` and `MultiCommon` combine peers. In an assembly feature `target` is `None`: the participants are the targets (§6.7).
- `tools` selects the other operands in source order (NX keeps tool order).
- `op` is `Join`, `Cut`, `Intersect`, `Assemble` (CATIA, by the tool's polarity), `UnionTrim` (below), or `Compound` (FreeCAD `Part::Compound`: `target: None`, the links in order as `tools`, `tools_after: Kept`; a repeated link is not repeated). `UnionTrim` joins the target and the tool, then removes each piece of one operand that lies outside the other operand's material and that the other operand encloses in some plane: every ray from the piece in that plane meets the other operand's material. A piece that belongs to both operands is kept. Whether a pick selects a piece on inputs no stored file known to the project shows is open (part 11), so the picks are Rule N case (a). The test is on whole pieces, and no plane through a point outside the other operand's convex hull encloses it, so a piece that reaches outside that hull is kept (a piece partly in an open pocket of the other operand, below). The source's picks are the faces its trim names, each with the face beside it where the source names one (CATIA union trim, which the CATIA Part Design guide states joins a body into the body it sits in and removes the pieces that faces to remove bound, or keeps the piece that faces to keep bound). The CATIA decoder keeps the picks, each with `catia:trim_form` (whether the source removes or keeps the piece the pick bounds), in the operation's `native_options` for the CATIA writer, and every other writer charges their loss (§3.4). The test is decidable on a finite set of planes per trim, the normals and axes of the other operand's faces. The hull test with the clause "unless every curved face of the other operand that bounds the piece is convex toward it" differs from the rule only on a void piece in an open notch or groove that touches a concave face, and on a void piece that touches only a convex wall but is enclosed by material it does not touch, and no stored file known to the project holds either shape in a trim (part 11). A tool piece that lies in an open pocket of the other operand, inside its hull, attached to parts that reach outside it, is one piece partly outside the hull, and the result keeps it. The file does not store either operand's solid as it stood before the trim, so testing the rule against the stored result takes a rebuild of both operands from their own features and a split of the two, which no decoder the contract describes performs. The CATIA decoder states `UnionTrim` on every union trim, from the feature's type, under Rule H1's clause for a rule the decoder cannot test (§3.1). The arm's meaning is that rule (part 11). A CATIA writer writes the picks back from `native_options`; a writer of another format writes the trim's stored result (§3.4, lowering step 3) unless it can evaluate the split. The picks are stored generic names (`ShortBrpLocation` labels over spec lists), not report tags, and the pieces of a face the trim divides share its name, so a face and its adjacent face can store one name. The picks decide no piece: a void piece that no pick bounds can be removed. The CATIA decoder consults no pick to decide a piece; it keeps the picks as stored, in `native_options`, which the CATIA writer writes back. A CATIA remove lump is a `DeleteFaces` (below).
- `tools_after` states what the source does with the tools: `Kept` leaves them as bodies (FreeCAD Part Booleans, Fusion and Inventor keep tools); `Consumed` removes them (Fusion, NX, SolidWorks, Inventor by default); `Absorbed` moves the tool body under the Boolean with its history editable (CATIA). Which bodies the current geometry holds is stated by the current states (§5.5) and never derived from this field.
- `new_component` states that the result goes into a new component that the feature makes: `occurrence` is the occurrence of the new component's definition, which the feature creates (§6.7, Existence), and that definition owns the result bodies in the state after the feature (§5.4). `None` states that the result stays with the target, as a source that stores the option off states it (§2.4), except where the operation keeps the native option `f3d:combine_new_component`: there the result goes into a new component whose occurrence is not read (below). Fusion stores the option as a Boolean of the combine's operand list. Which occurrence its new component is placed as is not read, so the Fusion decoder states `new_component: None` and keeps a set Boolean as the native option `f3d:combine_new_component` (typed, carrier unread; part 11). A writer whose target has no such option writes the combine and a placed occurrence of a new definition that holds its result, and charges a loss naming the feature.

**Split.** One operation splits bodies and faces, trims them, and cuts bodies with a surface.
- `ByTools` cuts `targets` with `tools` and leaves the tools unchanged: Fusion and Inventor split body, NX split body and trim body, SolidWorks cut with surface, split line, and standard trim, CATIA split of parts and surfaces, Fusion surface trim and split face, NX trim sheet, Inventor split and trim. `Plane` is a tool set of one member that is a datum, an origin plane, or a constructed plane. `Geometry` is every other tool set: it selects faces, sheet or solid bodies, curves, or sketches, and, where the source's tool set holds one beside other tools or holds several, datum or origin planes, each cutting as its whole plane, which `extend` does not change (a Fusion tool group that holds a work plane and faces). `targets` is `None` exactly in an assembly feature, whose participants are the targets (a CATIA assembly split, §6.7). A split that does not state `assembly`, whose targets the decoder did not read, has `Unread` picks.
- `extend` states whether the cut continues past where a `Geometry` tool reaches until it divides the targets. `Off` cuts only where the tool reaches (CATIA extrapolation type `None`; Fusion "Extend Splitting Tool(s)" off). `Extended` continues it by the law `method` states, §6.6's `ExtendMethod`: `Tangent` and `Curvature` are CATIA's extrapolation types, which continue the cut in tangency or in curvature up to the nearest free edges of the element cut (Generative Shape Design guide, Splitting Geometry; typed from the page, part 11); `method: None` where the source stores no law (Fusion split body and split face, which store one Boolean; part 11). `extend: None` means the source does not state it (§2.4). Fusion's split face stores the Boolean with its surface-intersection method only, so its decoder states `extend` there and `None` with a projection. Fusion's split body stores it whatever the tool: with a `Plane` tool, which is unbounded, both values give one result, and the value is the source setting `f3d:extend_splitting_tool` (Rule N case (b)).
- `Silhouette` cuts each target along its outline seen along the direction: on each target face, the curves where the face's normal is perpendicular to the direction, which follow the targets under every edit and are picked nowhere (Fusion Silhouette Split, a SolidWorks silhouette split line). The targets are their own tool, so `method` is `None`. `Kept::All { form: Some(Faces) }` divides the faces along those curves and leaves each body whole (Fusion's faces operation, result mode 0). Fusion's solid-body operation (mode 2) requires a planar outline and divides the body by the plane that holds it: it is `Kept::All { form: Some(Bodies) }` under Rule H1, stated only where every face the stored result adds lies on one plane that holds the outline, and `Kept::Native("f3d:silhouette_split_solid_body")` otherwise. Its shelled-body operation (mode 1) divides a shelled body in two by a cut through the wall that no text states: `Kept::Native("f3d:silhouette_split_shelled_body")` (Rule N case (a), part 11). A mode the decoder does not read is `kept: None`. The direction is that of the entity the source selects, a line's direction or a plane's or planar face's normal (Fusion's view direction, a construction axis, linear edge, planar face, or construction plane; a SolidWorks direction of pull, a plane), so the construction has one `Whole` `Parallel` input that picks it. Fusion stores the selector beside a solved model-space vector: the vector is `resolved`, and the pick is `Native` until the selector is joined to a record of the state before the split (typed, carrier unread; part 11). A SolidWorks silhouette split line also stores an angle, which SolidWorks' page names without defining the curves it gives: a split line whose angle is not zero is a `Native` operation (part 11).
- `method` states how the tools meet the targets: `Intersect` where tool surfaces cross them; `Project` where a curve tool reaches them along a projection (SolidWorks split line projection, Fusion split face along a vector, and closest point as `SurfaceNormal`).
- `Mutual` trims each element by the others and joins the kept pieces (CATIA two-element trim, SolidWorks mutual trim). A Creo merge in intersect mode is `Mutual` with a `Side` per quilt, each quilt's "side to keep"; a merge in join mode whose quilt overhangs the other's edge is `Mutual` with that quilt's `Side` and `None` for the other (PTC About the Merged Feature). A cut of a solid by a quilt is `ByTools` with the quilt as `Geometry` and a `Side` (SolidWorks cut with surface), and so is a Creo solidify that removes material, its side the material side (PTC About the Solidify Feature User Interface). Creo stores a merge's mode and sides in its role codes. The first quilt is always role 1300 with sign +1. A second role of 1302 or 1303 is intersect mode, whose quilts meet along class-223 intersection edges, and 1300 is join mode, whose quilts meet along boundary edges only.
