An intersect merge is `Mutual` over the two quilts with a `Side` flag each, read against each quilt's surface normal: the first flag is true where the second quilt's sign is +1, which keeps the second quilt on the side the first's surface normal points away from (−1 keeps the side it points to), and the second flag is true for role 1302, which keeps the first quilt on the side the second's surface normal points away from (1303 keeps the side it points to). The face normal does not separate the sides, so a decoder states each flag against the quilt's oriented normal from its surface normal and its orientation. A join merge is a `Knit` (§6.6). Role 1301 and the sign of a join, which chooses the side an overhanging quilt keeps, are not settled by any stored file known to the project and stay native options keyed `creo:<code>` (typed, carrier unread; part 11). A Creo solidify's form is read from its feature type and form bits: 917 with form 512 and instruction 1103 fills a quilt, 916 with 512 and 1103 removes material, 917 with form 640, the thin bit added, thickens it, and 943 with instructions 1104 and 40 replaces surfaces. The side the 1103 sign keeps is not decoded, since its quilt id joins no stored surface, and stays the native option `creo:1103` (typed, carrier unread; part 11).
- `Kept::All` keeps every piece, in the form `form` states: `Bodies` makes each piece a body of its own (Fusion and Inventor split body, NX split body, CATIA split keeping both sides, whose two results are separate elements), `Regions` keeps the pieces in one body as separate regions (FreeCAD Slice, a compound of the pieces in one object), and `Faces` keeps them as faces of their body (Fusion split face, SolidWorks split line). `None` means not read: a SolidWorks split-all trim (`moTrimRefSurface_c`), whose option bytes no stored file known to the project settles (part 11). A writer emits the target's split and charges a loss where the target's piece form differs. `Side { side }` keeps, for each side-defining tool or element, the side its oriented normal points to, or the other side where the flag is true (NX trim body, SolidWorks cut with surface, CATIA split and trim orientations, Inventor trim): `ByTools` holds one flag for its tools, and `Mutual` a list of one flag per element in element order, each `None` where the source does not state it. A `ByTools` split whose kept side the decoder did not read has `kept: None`. `Pieces` picks the kept or removed pieces. A piece pick targets the input face or body that the split cuts and locates the piece by its domain: `Fragment`, the `index`-th of `count` cells (§6.1), where the source numbers the cells of its partition (Fusion removed cells), and `Containing(point)` where the source locates a piece by a point (SolidWorks keep and remove selections, CATIA kept and removed sub-elements, whose BRep label stays in `native`). The witness holds the piece's cached geometry. `Native` keeps a source choice whose meaning is not established (Rule N case (a), part 11). A SolidWorks split keeps every piece, `All { form: Some(Bodies) }`, or, where it consumes pieces ("Consume cut bodies: Removes the body from the part"), `Pieces` with the consumed pieces in `remove`; each piece it saves to a new part is a `Stored` feature with a `Linked` origin in that part's scope, whose `source` picks the piece and whose `transform` holds the saved origin (Split and Save Bodies help and API `ISplitBodyFeatureData.SetSplitBodies2`).
- Pieces are named `Split { feature, from, piece }` (§5.7).

**Delete and keep bodies.** `DeleteSelected` removes the picked bodies; `KeepSelected` removes every other body of the anchored state, which at a current state's position is that state's extent (§5.5) (SolidWorks keep bodies).

**Extract.** `Extract` creates new geometry that copies the picked entities: bodies as bodies, faces as one sheet body, edges and curves as a wire body (NX extract body, face, and string; Creo copy surface; CATIA extract; Fusion copy-paste of bodies). A copy's entities are named `Instance { feature, instance: [1], of }` where the source names them by the entity they copy (§5.7). An extract anchored `Input` copies the source as it stands at the extract. A propagation rule is a `Picks::Rule` (CATIA tangent or point continuity as `Connected`; CATIA complementary extract as an `Of { kind: Face }` term minus the propagated term). A CATIA boundary is an extract of a `Boundary` rule term. A copy from another definition is a `Stored` feature with a `Linked` origin (§5.10). An extracted datum is a datum feature whose construction has one `Coincident` input that selects the source datum, with its `link` (§6.2). An NX extract not fixed at its timestamp evaluates after the last feature that changes its source, so the decoder places it there, anchored `Input`, whether NX stores it last or at its creation position (typed, carrier unread; part 11); its flag is the native option `nx:fix_at_timestamp`. NX's extract-body record (`EXTRBDY_feature_parms`) names the feature it copies from by its Part Navigator name and timeline number, and the flag is narrowed to one byte of its state lane, whose effect on geometry no stored file known to the project settles. A definition holds no `Current` anchor for it. NX's curve extract (`EXTRACT_STRING`, class `EXTRACT_string_parms`) holds one curve collector, its output curves, and optionally a rigid transform (`XFORM`). It is an `Extract` of the collector's edges and curves as a wire body, and where it holds a transform, that `Extract` followed by a `TransformBodies` copy of its wire body by the transform, two features. Every record owns its output curves; without a transform the outputs lie on their inputs, and with one they are the transform's rotation and translation of the inputs. The arm is under Rule H1: the NX decoder states either form where a record's outputs agree with it, and the record as a `Native` operation otherwise (part 11). `reversed: Some(true)` complements the copy's orientation: every face normal and edge direction is reversed, and a solid's material side is exchanged (FreeCAD `Part::Reverse`, a copy of its one source, `TopoDS_Shape::Reversed`, at the source's placement: `Part/App/PartFeatures.cpp` at 1.1.4). A writer whose target has no operation that reverses orientation writes the copy and charges a loss naming the feature.

**Transform bodies.**
- `Move` transforms the picked bodies in place, and they keep their identity. `Copy` leaves them and adds `count` copies: copy k, for k from 1 to `count`, applies the per-copy motion k times, and the per-copy motion is each step with its distance or angle divided by `divisions` (NX `Divisions`; a source that spreads one motion over its copies has `divisions` equal to `count`). `None` means not read, and since it decides how the stored distances and angles are read, a writer of another codec does not write them and charges a loss naming the feature (§2.4). `Translate`, `Components`, `PointToPoint`, and `Rotate` steps divide; a source that divides a motion with any other step is a `Native` operation. A SolidWorks copy divides one translation or one rotation: where both are stated it applies only the rotation, and it copies only those (API `IFeatureManager.InsertMoveCopyBody2` and the Move/Copy Body help). Copy k's entities are named `Instance { feature, instance: [k], of }` where the source names them by the entity they copy (§5.7). A SolidWorks Move/Copy Body names copy k's faces `Copy(P, k, <name>)` (`moCopySurfIdRep_c`), whose producer is the copying feature and whose field is the copy's step, 1 to the copy count, so it is `Instance { feature: P, instance: [k], of: <name> }`; a Surface Cut's copy hops keep their field in `NameEntry.native` (part 11). A pick of a `Component` moves that occurrence (a Fusion Move of components); each state in which its placement differs from the placement its configuration resolves to states it, in `delta.poses` (§5.4) or, for the current state, in `CurrentState.poses` (§5.5).
- `steps` apply in order. `Translate` moves along a direction by a distance; `Components` by three distances along a frame's axes (NX delta XYZ, CATIA coordinates with a reference axis system, SolidWorks translate values); `PointToPoint` and `FrameToFrame` move one reference onto another (NX, CATIA); `Rotate` turns about an axis (NX, CATIA, SolidWorks, Inventor); `Scale` scales about a locus (Fusion, SolidWorks, CATIA, Draft clones); `Fixed` is a transform the source stores without any construction (Fusion move, Inventor free drag). NX distance-angle is a translate step and a rotate step. `Constrained` places the moved bodies where its mates hold: each `BodyMate` relates a connector on a moved body to fixed geometry by one of the joint kinds `Coincident`, `Parallel`, `Perpendicular`, `Tangent`, `Concentric`, `Distance`, or `Angle` (§6.7), with its alignment, and `resolved` holds the solved transform (SolidWorks move or copy of bodies by constraints: "The selected bodies move as a single entity. The bodies that are not selected are treated as fixed", the Move/Copy Body help and API `IMoveCopyBodyFeatureData.AddMate`). Mate sets that SolidWorks applies in turn are one step each, in order. A writer whose target has no body mates writes `Fixed(resolved)` and charges a loss naming the feature.
- `resolved` is the composed transform in the state the steps are anchored in: a cache (K2) of the steps.
- A reflection alone is not a transformation step: a source feature that mirrors bodies is a `Pattern` with `Bodies` seeds and a `Mirror` layout, never a `Scale`. A `Scale` step states the factors its source stores; a negative factor scales by its magnitude and reflects along its axis, or through `center` where the factor is uniform, as the source's own scale does (a Draft clone, whose `Scale` is a free vector).
- An extract without motion is `Extract`; `TransformBodies` always has a step.

**Direct edit.**
- `MoveFaces` moves faces rigidly by a transformation (NX move face, Fusion MoveFace). An offset of faces along their normals is an `Offset` with a `Move` result (§6.4).
- `DeleteFaces` removes faces. `Open` leaves the gap open, so the result is a sheet (Fusion surface delete face); `Extend` closes it by extending the neighbouring faces (Fusion delete face, SolidWorks delete and patch, NX delete face, CATIA remove face). `Fill` closes it with one new face bounded by the gap's edges, meeting each neighbouring face with contact where `tangent` is `Some(false)` and tangent to it where `Some(true)`; its interior is the writer's patch, as for `Patch` (§6.6). SolidWorks' delete and delete and patch are `Open` and `Extend`. Its delete and fill is `Fill`, its tangent fill `tangent`, typed from SolidWorks' Delete Face PropertyManager page ("Deletes faces and generates a single face to close any gap"; "Tangent fill cleared. The fill use contact edges. Tangent fill selected. The fill uses tangent edges."). No stored file known to the project holds a delete-face feature that fills, and the option lies past face references not framed, so the decoder states `Fill` only where the state at the feature's mark shows a new face, with `tangent: None`, and keeps the option as `sldprt:delete_fill` and `sldprt:tangent_fill` (typed, carrier unread, part 11). A writer whose target has no delete and fill takes step 3 (§3.4), since the gap's edges exist only between a delete and a patch. Deleting every face of a closed shell leaves no gap: a void shell's cavity is filled, and a region whose exterior shell is deleted is removed. A CATIA remove lump is such a deletion: its faces to remove pick the lumps to delete by a `Region` term with no boundary seeded by them, and its faces to keep make every other shell of the body the deletion, an `All { kind: Face }` term excluding the kept lumps ("either you specify the faces you wish to remove or conversely, the faces you wish to keep", the CATIA Part Design guide).
- `ReplaceFaces` replaces `faces` with the faces of `replacement` (Creo replace, Fusion and NX replace face).

**Graft.** `Graft` replaces part of a body's boundary by a sheet whose boundary lies on the body: the sheet's boundary divides the body's boundary, and the result's material lies on the side of the sheet its normal points to, the other side where `flip` is true, so material is added where the sheet lies outside the body and removed where it lies inside. `simplify` merges connected faces that share a surface. Sources: CATIA sew surface ("a boolean operation combining a surface with a body. This capability adds or removes material by modifying the surface of the solid", the CATIA Part Design guide) and Creo solidify replace surface ("Replaces a portion of the solid surfaces with the selected quilt. Only available if the selected quilt boundaries lie on solid geometry", PTC). A writer whose target has no such operation cannot choose between its replace-face and surface-cut operations: which gives the same result depends on where the sheet lies against the body, inside or outside, which no writer decides without a kernel, so step 3 applies (§3.4).

#### Flex

```rust
pub struct Flex {
    pub bodies: SetSelection,
    pub frame: Construction<Frame>,
    pub trims: [Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>>; 2],
    pub kind: FlexKind,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum FlexKind {
    Bend    { angle: Dimension<Angle>, radius: Option<Dimension<PositiveLength>> },
    Twist   { angle: Dimension<Angle> },
    Taper   { factor: Dimension<FiniteReal> },
    Stretch { distance: Dimension<Length> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
```

- `Flex` deforms `bodies` between two trim planes normal to the z axis of `frame` (SolidWorks' triad), which start at the bodies' extents along that axis and move inward by `trims`, and changes only the region between them (SolidWorks Flex PropertyManager and Flex overview; typed from that description, part 11). `Bend` bends about the frame's x axis with its neutral plane the frame's xz plane, keeping the arc length between the trim planes along that plane, so that length is `angle` times the bend radius, and `radius` is a cache (K2) of the two where the source stores it. `Twist` turns about the z axis by `angle`, `Taper` tapers along it by `factor`, and `Stretch` stretches along it by `distance`. SolidWorks' hard edges and flex accuracy choose how one deformation is represented, source settings (Rule N case (b)).
- How a twist or a taper varies between the trim planes, what a taper factor scales, which trim plane a stretch keeps, and whether material beyond the trims moves rigidly are not settled by any stored file known to the project, so the deformation is the feature's evaluation (K2), the state after it where the document holds one (part 11). A writer whose target has no flex writes that state as stored geometry (§3.4 step 3).

### 6.6 Surfacing, wireframe, forms, sheet metal, and meshes

These operations build and edit sheets and wires, own subdivision cages, form sheet metal, and edit meshes: `Patch`, `Knit`, `Unsew`, `UnsewFaces`, `Extend`, `ImplicitSweep`, `BoundaryFill`, `Curve`, `Form`, `SheetMetal`, and `Mesh`. Surfaces built through sections are lofts (§6.3). An offset surface is an `Offset` with a `Copy` result (§6.4). Trimming and splitting sheets is `Split` (§6.5). An explicit sweep with a positioned profile is a `Sweep` (§6.3).

#### Patch

A patch spans a closed boundary, optionally through passing elements, around inner boundaries. A planar patch is a patch with `planar: Some(true)`.

```rust
pub struct Patch {
    pub bounds: PatchBounds,
    pub passing: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub planar: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub simplified: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub output: SheetOutput,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum PatchBounds { Profile(ProfileRef), Loops { outer: Vec<PatchEdge>, inner: Vec<Vec<PatchEdge>> } }
pub struct PatchEdge { pub curve: PathRef, pub condition: Option<SectionCondition> }
```

- `Profile` bounds a patch by sketch regions or faces, with the region's holes as inner boundaries and no edge conditions (SolidWorks planar surface from a sketch, Inventor boundary patch from a sketch). `Loops` lists boundary segments in traversal order, each with its own condition (CATIA fill, SolidWorks filled surface, Fusion surface patch, NX fill hole, Creo fill surface, Inventor boundary patch). A boundary condition is §6's `SectionCondition`: `Free` is contact, `Tangent` and `Curvature` meet the `support` faces (CATIA fill supports; SolidWorks contact, tangent, and curvature per edge).
- `passing` selects curves and points the patch passes through (CATIA passing elements, SolidWorks constraint curves).
- `planar` states that the patch is the plane through its boundary (CATIA `PlaneOnly`, SolidWorks planar surface).
- A Fusion surface patch stores a byte that reverses the normal of the whole surface it makes. Which side the normal faces where the byte is 0 is not stated against the boundary or any other reference, so the byte is the native option `f3d:patch_reverse_normal` (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- `simplified: Some(true)` makes the patch one degree-3 surface bounded by its own edges, not cut out of a larger surface by parameter-space curves: bicubic over a four-sided boundary, cubic by linear between the two curves of a two-sided boundary, and a plane over a planar boundary. Its span count is not fixed. Over a boundary of another form the patch is one degree-3 surface trimmed by the boundary, and which surface is not established: there the decoder states the flag as stored, and a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the patch. `Some(false)` lets the source fit its default patch. SolidWorks' filled-surface optimize is `simplified` (tail byte a+6 of `moFillRefSurface_c`, the tail anchored on its constant `41 82`): with it set a B-surface patch is degree 3, with it clear degree 5, and the byte, not the boundary's side count, makes the difference. A writer whose target cannot ask for such a patch writes its default patch and charges `export:feature.lowered`. SolidWorks' fix up boundary is the native option `sldprt:fill_fixup`, with tail byte a+23 of the fill record read into it. That the byte is the option is not established, and both effects the vendor's page gives fix-up, partial use of a selected edge longer than the patch side and a built closing piece across a gap in the boundary, occur with the byte clear; no stored file known to the project says whether the optimized patch closes the gap of itself or the byte has another meaning or polarity (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- `output.solid` carries the SolidWorks filled surface's "try to form solid", and a `Sew` Boolean its "merge result", which knits the patch into the surfaces it meets (§6). SolidWorks stores the output in tail byte a+18 of the fill record: 0 a new sheet, 1 knitted into the sheet it meets, 2 knitted and closed into a solid.

#### Knit

A knit joins sheets, wires, or solids along shared boundaries.

```rust
pub struct Knit {
    pub elements: OrderedSelection,
    pub tolerance: Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>>,
    pub simplify: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub healing: Option<Healing>,
    pub federation: Option<SetSelection>,
    pub output: SheetOutput,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub struct Healing {
    pub objective: Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>>,
    pub tangency: Option<Dimension<Angle>>,
    pub tangency_objective: Option<Dimension<Angle>>,
    pub frozen: Option<SetSelection>,
}
```

- Sources: CATIA join, SolidWorks knit, Fusion stitch, NX sew, Inventor stitch, CATIA close surface with `solid: Some(CapPlanarOpenings)`. A Creo merge in join mode whose quilts meet along their single-sided edges is a `Knit`, and a Creo solidify that fills a quilt with solid is a `Knit` with `solid: Some(IfClosed)` and a `Join` (PTC About the Merged Feature and About the Solidify Feature User Interface); until the role bits and the solidify bit are read (part 11), the decoder keeps such a feature `Native` with its codes as native options keyed `creo:<code>`. A composite curve is a knit of curves (SolidWorks composite curve, Creo composite datum curve, CATIA join of curves).
- `elements` keeps source order: the first quilt of a Creo merge stated as a `Knit` is its primary. Sub-elements the source removes from the joined result (CATIA `SubElementsToRemove`) are the `excluded` terms of a `Rule` selection over the elements (§5.8).
- `tolerance` is the largest gap the knit closes (CATIA `MergeDist` and `CloseTolerance`, SolidWorks gap control, Fusion `StitchingTolerence`, NX sew tolerance). `simplify` merges coincident faces and edges of the result (SolidWorks merge entities, CATIA `Simplify`). `healing` deforms the elements so that gaps up to `tolerance` close, leaving a gap of at most `objective`, and, where `tangency` is stated, tangent discontinuities up to that angle, leaving at most `tangency_objective`; the `frozen` elements are not deformed (CATIA healing, the Generative Shape Design guide: "Elements between which the gap is larger than the indicated value are not processed"). The deformation is the source's, and the result is its evaluation; a writer whose target has no healing writes the knit and charges a loss naming the feature.
- `federation` groups elements of the knit's result so that a later pick of any one of them reaches the group (§5.8): a rule selection over the result whose seeds are the elements the source names, with `Propagation::Off` for the seeds alone, `Connected { continuity: Some(G0) }` for every element joined to them with point continuity, `Connected { continuity: Some(G1) }` for every element joined to them with tangent continuity, or an `Of` term on the knit's own result for every element of it, `kind: Face` where the knit joins surfaces and `kind: Edge` where it joins curves; `None` states no group. CATIA's federation is this, typed from Dassault's page Joining Surfaces or Curves (CATIA V5-6R2025 user guide; its modes All, Point continuity, Tangent continuity, and No propagation, and a worked example in which an up-to-surface pad recomputes on another face of the group after an edit).

#### Unsew

An unsew cuts a sheet apart along edges, or cuts faces out of it.

```rust
pub struct Unsew { pub edges: SetSelection, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub struct UnsewFaces { pub faces: SetSelection, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
```

- `Unsew` cuts a sheet in two along `edges`: the picked edges divide the sheet into two pieces, and the faces on the two sides become two sheet bodies, each with its own copy of the picked edges, the input body keeping one side and a new body holding the other. The arm is under Rule H1: a decoder states `Unsew` only where the stored result after it is two bodies so divided, and the source's unsew as a `Native` operation otherwise. NX's unsew by edge (`UnsewParms`) is so (part 11). That the operand is an edge is read from the lane's node id, which is that edge's and no face's. Which side keeps the input body is not ruled (part 11). A writer whose target has no unsew writes each side as an extracted sheet and charges a loss naming the feature.
- `UnsewFaces` cuts each face `faces` picks out of its body as a sheet body of its own, with its own copies of its edges; the faces left behind keep the input body, open where the picked faces were. It is not an operand form of `Unsew`: an unsew by edges divides a sheet into two pieces at the edges, and an unsew by faces makes one body per picked face. Fusion's unstitch is `UnsewFaces`: it separates exactly the picked faces, each into a surface body. Its other controls are native options (Rule N case (a), part 11). Whether NX's unsew by faces makes one body per face or one body of the picked set is not established, so it stays `Native` (part 11). A writer whose target has no such operation writes each picked face as an extracted sheet and the rest of the body as the body, and charges a loss naming the feature.

#### Extend

```rust
pub struct Extend {
    pub edges: SetSelection,
    pub limit: Option<ExtendLimit>,
    pub method: Option<ExtendMethod>,
    pub output: Option<SheetOutput>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum ExtendLimit { Distance(Dimension<Length>), UpTo(SetSelection), Natural, Native(NonBlankString) }
pub enum ExtendMethod { Natural, Tangent, Curvature, Perpendicular, Native(NonBlankString) }
```

- `edges` selects free boundary edges of sheets; a source that extends whole faces uses an `Of { kind: Edge }` term with face seeds. `UpTo` extends to a point or a surface (SolidWorks, CATIA `Until`). `Natural` extends to the carrier's natural boundary: the face covers its surface's untrimmed domain, its holes and outer trims removed, or the loops `edges` picks only, and a wire's edge covers its curve (SolidWorks untrim surface by extending edges, "extending an existing surface along its natural boundaries", Untrim Surface help; CATIA untrim, which restores "the initial surface" of a face, or one picked loop only, and an infinite or closed initial surface to its bounding box, the FreeStyle guide). SolidWorks untrim's percentage of the natural boundary and its connect-endpoints form are native options (`sldprt:untrim_distance`, `sldprt:connect_endpoints`): no stored file known to the project settles what the percentage measures or what the surface connect endpoints builds (Rule N case (a), part 11). `output` states whether the result merges with the original (`Apply` with `Sew`) or is a body of its own (`NewBody`) (SolidWorks untrim's merge with original).
- `Natural` continues the underlying surface (SolidWorks same surface, Fusion natural); `Tangent` extends linearly (SolidWorks linear, CATIA tangent, Fusion tangent); `Curvature` extrapolates with curvature continuity (CATIA); `Perpendicular` extends normal to the boundary (Fusion). Sources: CATIA extrapolate, SolidWorks extend surface, Fusion surface extend, NX extend sheet, Creo extend.

#### Implicit-section sweeps

The section of these sweeps is a line or a circle that the operation builds at each spine station from guides, supports, directions, and laws. Ruled surfaces grown from edges are line sweeps.

```rust
pub struct ImplicitSweep {
    pub section: ImplicitSection,
    pub spine: Option<PathRef>,
    pub limits: SpineLimits,
    pub solution: Option<u32>,
    pub corner: Option<CornerTransition>,
    pub output: SolidOutput,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum ImplicitSection {
    Line { mode: LineMode, lengths: [Option<LineLength>; 2] },
    Circle(CircleMode),
    Conic { guides: Vec<PathRef>, supports: [Option<SetSelection>; 2], parameter: Option<Law<Fraction>> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum LineMode {
    TwoGuides   { first: PathRef, second: PathRef },
    Middle      { guide: PathRef, middle: PathRef },
    Surface     { guide: PathRef, reference: FaceReference, from: Option<SurfaceRelation>, angle: Option<Law<Angle>> },
    Curve       { guide: PathRef, curve: PathRef, from: Option<CurveRelation>, angle: Option<Law<Angle>> },
    Direction   { guide: PathRef, direction: Construction<Direction>, from: Option<DirectionRelation>, angle: Option<Law<Angle>> },
    TangentTo   { guide: PathRef, surface: SetSelection },
    TwoTangents { first: SetSelection, second: SetSelection },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum FaceReference { Faces(SetSelection), Adjacent { alternate: Option<Dimension<bool>> } }
pub enum SurfaceRelation { Tangent, Normal }
pub enum DirectionRelation { Parallel, Perpendicular }
pub enum CurveRelation { TowardReference }
pub enum LineLength { Law(Law<Length>), UpTo(SetSelection), Native(NonBlankString) }
pub enum CircleMode {
    ThreeGuides        { guides: [PathRef; 3] },
    TwoGuidesRadius    { guides: [PathRef; 2], radius: Law<Length> },
    CenterAngles       { center: PathRef, reference: PathRef, from: Option<CurveRelation>, angles: [Option<Law<Angle>>; 2] },
    CenterRadius       { center: PathRef, radius: Law<Length> },
    TangentTwoGuides   { passing: PathRef, limit: PathRef, surface: SetSelection },
    TangentGuideRadius { passing: PathRef, surface: SetSelection, radius: Law<Length>, trim: Option<Dimension<bool>> },
    TangentLimitRadius { limit: PathRef, surface: SetSelection, radius: Law<Length>, angles: [Option<Law<Angle>>; 2] },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
```

The section at each spine station lies in the plane normal to the spine there, and each guide, surface, or direction acts through its point or trace in that plane. The modes are CATIA's (`HybridShapeSweepLine.Mode` and `HybridShapeSweepCircle.Mode` of the V5 automation reference, as the pycatia mirror publishes it; `Choice`). CATIA stores each mode as the automation mode plus one: line sweeps store 2 with two guide curves, 5 with a reference surface and an angle, and 7 with a draft direction; circle sweeps store 7, 8, and 10 as the automation mode plus one, while a stored 4 does not fit and is `CircleMode::Native("catia:circle:4")` (below); and the SolidWorks and Fusion ruled surfaces use two of the line modes.

- `spine: None` states that the source names no spine; CATIA then uses the first guide. `limits` are the relimiting elements on the spine (`RelimElem1/2`, §6.3). `solution` selects among the solutions the source enumerates (`SolutionNumber`). The output is a sheet unless `output.body` says otherwise.
- **Lines.** `TwoGuides` is the segment between the two guides' points (CATIA mode 1). `Middle` is the segment from the guide's point whose midpoint is the middle curve's point (mode 3). `Curve` is the line through the guide's point at `angle` from the direction `from` names (mode 2, "a guide curve and an angle"): `TowardReference` is the direction toward the reference curve's point. No stored file known to the project settles which direction CATIA measures from, so the CATIA decoder states `from: None`; `from` decides how the stored angle is read, so where it is `None` a writer of another codec does not write the angle and charges a loss naming the feature (§2.4, part 11). `TangentTo` is the line from the guide's point tangent to `surface` (mode 5), and `TwoTangents` the line tangent to both surfaces (mode 7); `solution` chooses among tangents.
- `Surface` holds the line at `angle` from the reference surface's tangent or normal plane along the guide (mode 4): CATIA reference surface with its angle law, whose zero the CATIA decoder states as `from` once a decoded file establishes it (the documentation measures it from the projected surface normal, which favours `Normal`) and `None` until then; SolidWorks and Fusion ruled surfaces "tangent to surface" and "normal to surface" are `Tangent` and `Normal` with `reference: Adjacent`, where `alternate` picks the second face at the guide edge. `from` decides how the stored angle is read, so where it is `None` a writer of another codec does not write the angle and charges a loss naming the feature (§2.4).
- `Direction` holds the line at `angle` from a draft direction (mode 6; CATIA draft direction, SolidWorks "tapered to vector", Fusion direction); SolidWorks "perpendicular to vector" is `from: Some(Perpendicular)`.
- `lengths` are the line's extents on either side of its first point: a length law, or up to an element (CATIA `DefType`, `DefElem`, `FirstLengthLaw`, `SecondLengthLaw`).
- **Circles.** `ThreeGuides` is the circle through the three guides' points, and `solution` chooses which of its arcs (CATIA mode 2, four solutions). `TwoGuidesRadius` is the circle of `radius` through the two guides' points (mode 3). The CATIA decoder does not read a stored 4 as it: a stored 4 holds one guide and a radius, so the decoder states `CircleMode::Native("catia:circle:4")` (Rule N case (a), part 11). `CenterAngles` is the circle centred at the center curve's point through the reference curve's point, between the two `angles` measured from the direction `from` names, `TowardReference` being the radius to that point, the whole circle where both are `None` (mode 5). No stored file known to the project holds a circle sweep of this mode with an angle, so the CATIA decoder states `from: None`, and a writer of another codec does not write the angles (§2.4, part 11). `CenterRadius` is the circle of `radius` centred at the center curve's point (mode 6); an angle law the source stores on it stays a native option until its zero is established (Rule N case (a), part 11). `TangentTwoGuides` passes through the `passing` guide's point and touches `surface` tangentially along the `limit` guide (mode 7), and `TangentGuideRadius` has `radius`, passes through the `passing` guide's point, and touches `surface` tangentially (mode 8). `trim` on `TangentGuideRadius` trims the tangency surface by the sweep and assembles with it the portion that makes the result tangent (CATIA "Trim with tangency surface"). `TangentLimitRadius` has `radius` and touches `surface` along the `limit` curve, which lies on it: its centre lies on the surface's normal at the limit curve's point, at `radius` from it, and it runs between the two `angles`, measured from the surface's tangent plane, the whole circle where both are `None` (CATIA limit curve and tangency surface, the Generative Shape Design guide's circular-profile subtypes). The automation reference lists modes 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 8. CATIA stores the limit-curve subtype as 10 (automation 9): it is the only stored mode with one curve, one reference surface, a radius, and two relimiting angles (part 11). No stored file known to the project holds automation modes 1 and 4 (stored 2 and 5), so what they are is not established, and the decoder states `CircleMode::Native("catia:circle:<stored>")` for them (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- `corner` states how the result passes a sharp corner of its guide chain, as a sweep's `transition` does (§6.3): Fusion ruled surface corner type `0` rounded is `Round` and `1` mitered `Mitre`. A SolidWorks ruled surface with its connecting surfaces cleared is `Open`, a gap the full ruling length between two faces that touch at the corner point; with them set, it is `CornerTransition::Native("sldprt:connecting_surface")`, since no stored file known to the project settles the shape of the surface it builds at a sharp corner. The record's closing fields are its type, its distance and angle, and three option words: `d` goes with trim and knit, which leaves `b` for the connecting surface (inferred). The cleared state is under Rule H1: the SolidWorks decoder states `corner: Some(CornerTransition::Open)` only where `b` is 0 at a corner whose stored faces leave a gap, and `corner: None` at every other corner, and keeps the three words as the native options `sldprt:ruled_option_b`, `sldprt:ruled_option_c`, and `sldprt:ruled_option_d` (part 11). The corner that would show the set state is such a gapped corner saved with the option set (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- A circle swept along a path with a constant stated diameter (NX tube, Fusion pipe) is a `Sweep` of a generated `Circle` section (§6.3). `Conic` is, in each plane normal to the spine, the conic arc from the first guide's point to the last's through the points of the guides between, two to five guides in order; `supports` holds the surface each end is tangent to, where one is stated; and `parameter` is the ratio OM/OT that places a passing point M on the line from the midpoint O of the chord to the apex T of the end tangents, 0.5 a parabola, below it an ellipse, above it a hyperbola, which fixes a two-guide conic (CATIA conical profile and conic curve, the Generative Shape Design guide). A tangent angle the source states "in relation to the support" stays a native option, since no stored file known to the project settles its zero (Rule N case (a), part 11). CATIA's adaptive sweep (`GSMSweepSketch`) is `ImplicitSection::Native("catia:GSMSweepSketch")` (Rule N case (a), part 11). It re-solves a section sketch in the plane normal to the spine at each point of a guide, and at each station, a point on the guide, it restates some of that sketch's dimensional constraints with values of the station's own. CATIA stores it as a base section sketch that owns one user-section sketch per station, each with an index and a reference to its station point and owning a copy of a base dimension record per value it sets. Each station keeps the base sketch's constraints and stores its own solved section, so a station that sets no value for a constraint has the value its stored section holds. The law by which a value varies between stations is not established. Without it the section at a point of the guide cannot be constructed, so no arm states the sweep. The decoder keeps, in the sweep's native options, the guide (`catia:adaptive_guide`), the base section sketch (`catia:adaptive_section`), and for each station its point (`catia:adaptive_station.<i>`) and each value it sets (`catia:adaptive_station.<i>.<constraint>`, a length or an angle that a parameter may drive), so a CATIA writer writes the sweep back with its stations editable; a writer of another codec takes step 3 (§3.4) and charges a loss naming the sweep.

#### Boundary fill

```rust
pub struct BoundaryFill {
    pub tools: SetSelection,
    pub cells: Vec<SetSelection>,
    pub regions: Option<RegionKind>,
    pub cap_planar: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub merge: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
    pub tools_after: Option<ToolDisposition>,
    pub boolean: Option<Boolean>,
    pub native_options: NativeOptions,
    pub source_settings: NativeOptions,
}
pub enum RegionKind { Intersecting, Internal, Both }
```

- `tools` partition space into cells. Each entry of `cells` selects one kept cell by a `Containing(point)` pick (Fusion boundary fill; SolidWorks intersect, `moSculpt_c`, whose result faces carry their cell in a signed field of their names that the intersect record's region entries repeat, so its decoder makes one cell of each field that heads a group of side faces; the record's cell order and the form of an excluded region stay in its native record, part 11). `regions` states which cells the tools make: `Intersecting` the closed volumes that the union or the intersection of the tools bounds, `Internal` the closed hollow volumes inside them, `Both` both; `cap_planar` first closes the planar openings of sheet tools; `merge: Some(true)` makes touching kept cells one body, and `Some(false)` each kept cell a body of its own (Fusion boundary fill); `tools_after` states what becomes of the tools (SolidWorks consume surfaces is `Consumed`) (SolidWorks Intersect help and API `IIntersectFeatureData`).

#### Wireframe

Curves that are design geometry are curve features. Points, lines, planes, and frames used as references are datums (§6.2).

```rust
pub struct CurveFeature { pub definition: CurveDefinition, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
pub enum CurveDefinition {
    Spline(SplineCurve),
    Helix(Helix),
    Projection { source: SetSelection, onto: SetSelection, direction: Option<ProjectionDirection> },
    Intersection { first: SetSelection, second: SetSelection },
    Bridge { ends: [BridgeEnd; 2] },
    Text(TextCurve),
    Constructed(Construction<Curve>),
    Corner { arc: Construction<Curve>, trim: Option<Dimension<bool>> },
    Polygon { placement: Construction<Frame>, sides: Dimension<u32>, circumradius: Dimension<PositiveLength> },
    Point(Construction<Point>),
    Equation { frame: Construction<Frame>, coordinates: EquationCoordinates },
    Combined { first: CombineOperand, second: CombineOperand, nearest: Option<Dimension<bool>> },
    Offset {
        curve: OrderedSelection,
        support: SetSelection,
        offset: CurveOffset,
        measure: Option<OffsetMeasure>,
        corner: Option<CornerTransition>,
        smoothing: Option<Continuity>,
    },
    Smoothed {
        curve: OrderedSelection,
        max_deviation: Option<Dimension<NonNegativeLength>>,
        tangency_threshold: Option<Dimension<Angle>>,
        curvature_ratio: Option<Dimension<Fraction>>,
        continuity: Option<Continuity>,
    },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub enum EquationCoordinates {
    Cartesian   { x: Law<Length>, y: Law<Length>, z: Law<Length> },
    Cylindrical { r: Law<Length>, theta: Law<Angle>, z: Law<Length> },
    Spherical   { rho: Law<Length>, theta: Law<Angle>, phi: Law<Angle> },
    Native(NonBlankString),
}
pub struct SplineCurve { pub points: Vec<SplinePoint>, pub closed: Option<Dimension<bool>>, pub support: Option<SetSelection> }
pub struct SplinePoint { pub point: Construction<Point>, pub tangent: Option<Construction<Direction>>, pub tension: Option<Dimension<PositiveReal>> }
pub struct BridgeEnd {
    pub curve: OrderedSelection,
    pub at: Option<Construction<Point>>,
    pub continuity: Option<Continuity>,
    pub tension: Option<Dimension<PositiveReal>>,
    pub reversed: Option<Dimension<bool>>,
}
pub struct TextCurve { pub text: TextContent, pub placement: TextPlacement }
pub enum TextPlacement { Plane(Construction<Frame>), OnCurve { path: PathRef }, OnFace { faces: SetSelection, path: PathRef } }
pub struct CombineOperand { pub curve: OrderedSelection, pub direction: Option<Construction<Direction>> }
pub enum CurveOffset { Law(Law<Length>), Through(Construction<Point>) }
pub enum OffsetMeasure { Euclidean, Geodesic }
```

- `Spline` passes through constructed points with optional tangent directions and magnitudes (CATIA spline, SolidWorks curve through points, Creo interpolated datum curve). A spline on a support lies on it.
- `Helix` is §6.3's helix (CATIA, SolidWorks, FreeCAD `Part::Helix`, NX helix). A helix whose axis the decoder cannot resolve has a placement with one input whose `role` is `None` and whose reference is the source's selection of the axis, `Unread` or a `Native` pick (§5.8; §5.9, Unread roles), and no resolved value.
- `Projection` projects curves and points onto faces (CATIA projection, NX project curve, FreeCAD project on surface). An NX projection that is its own feature (`CPROJ`) is a `Curve` feature with `Projection`, also where a sketch consumes it; the sketch entity is `Derived` from that feature's result (§6.1). `Intersection` intersects two sets of surfaces, curves, or planes (CATIA intersection, NX intersection curve, FreeCAD `Part::Section`).
- `Bridge` joins two curves at points with an end continuity each (NX bridge curve, CATIA connect curve). `at` is the connection point where the source states one other than the curve end.
- `TextCurve.text` holds the content, font, and size in the sketch text form (§6.1) (NX text; FreeCAD Draft `ShapeString`, a `Plane` text curve).
- `Constructed` is a line segment, arc, or circle built from references by a construction (§5.9): CATIA GSD lines (point-point, point-direction, angle to curve, normal to surface, bisecting, tangent) and circles (center-radius, center-point, two and three points, bitangent, tritangent, center-axis, with limits and a support). A `Construction<Curve>` takes the subjects `Whole` and `Origin`; the origin of a circle or arc is its center, of a line segment its start. FreeCAD fixed line and arc primitives are `Constructed` curves with no inputs and a resolved value.
- `Polygon` is the closed wire of a regular polygon of `sides` vertices on the circle of `circumradius` about the frame's z axis in its xy plane, as `PrimitiveShape::Prism` places its base (FreeCAD `Part::RegularPolygon`, `PrimitiveFeature.cpp`). `Point` is a wire body that holds one free vertex at the constructed point (FreeCAD `Part::Vertex`).
- `Equation` is the curve whose point at each `t` from 0 to 1 has the `coordinates` in `frame`: Cartesian `x`, `y`, `z`; cylindrical radius `r`, angle `theta` about z from x toward y, and height `z`; or spherical radius `rho`, polar angle `theta` from the frame's +z axis, and azimuth `phi` about z from x toward y, the point being `rho`·(sin `theta` cos `phi`, sin `theta` sin `phi`, cos `theta`). Each coordinate is a `Law` over the curve parameter (§6), whose `Expression` form uses `LawParameter` as `t`. A Creo curve from equation is one (relations in `t` such as `r=9*(1-t)` and `theta=-t*3*360+90`): its coordinate system is the frame's input, each coordinate is the expression its relations assign it, with any intermediate assignment substituted, under Creo's unit-blind rule (§5.13). Creo states the coordinate kind as the curve feature's placement instruction, 4132 Cartesian, 4133 cylindrical, and 4134 spherical, and as the curve entity's `csys_type`, 1, 2, and 4, where its release writes one, and evaluates its angles in degrees; a binary model holds its relations as a compiled tree whose statements a decoder rebuilds. The spherical convention above is open (part 11). A writer whose target has no equation curve writes a spline through points it evaluates, which matches the curve only at those points, and charges a loss naming the feature.
- `Combined` is the curve where the extrusions of two curves meet: each curve extruded along its `direction`, or normal to its own plane where `direction` is `None`; `nearest: Some(true)` keeps, of several solutions, the one nearest the first curve (CATIA combine, normal and along directions, the Generative Shape Design guide).
- `Offset` is the curve on `support` each of whose points lies at the offset distance from `curve`, a constant or a law along it (`Law`), or through a point (`Through`); `measure` is `Euclidean`, the straight distance whatever the support, or `Geodesic`, measured on the support; `corner` closes a convex corner sharp (`Mitre`) or by the arc a ball rolling on the curve leaves (`Round`); `smoothing` makes the result tangent or curvature continuous (CATIA parallel curve, whose law offsets are Euclidean).
- `Smoothed` is a curve within `max_deviation` of `curve`, which fits in a pipe of that radius about it, whose point, tangency, and curvature discontinuities below its thresholds are smoothed: a tangency discontinuity below `tangency_threshold`, and a curvature discontinuity where ‖ρ₁ − ρ₂‖ / ‖ρ₂‖ < (1 − r)/r for `curvature_ratio` r; `continuity` is the continuity the source forces everywhere, `None` for CATIA's threshold mode (CATIA curve smooth). The fit is the source's, and the curve is its evaluation.
- `Corner` is a corner of two elements: `arc` is the arc of its radius tangent to both, on a support where it has one, built as a construction (§5.9). `trim: Some(true)` makes the result one wire: the first element up to its tangency point, the arc, and the second element from its tangency point, each element keeping the piece that makes the wire tangent-continuous there; `Some(false)` makes the result the arc alone (CATIA corner `Trim`: 2 true, 1 false). Which piece of each element the wire keeps is inferred from tangent continuity, since the wires are not decoded (part 11). A writer whose target's corner does not trim its elements writes the arc and charges a loss naming the feature where `trim` is true.
- CATIA blend support trimming is a section's `trim_support` (§6.3). Every blend limit stores the `TrimSupport` field; `Border`, beside it, is an enumeration (2 and 3), not the support.

#### Subdivision form

```rust
pub struct Form { pub cage: Topology, pub native_options: NativeOptions, pub source_settings: NativeOptions }
```

- A form owns its control cages as a `Topology` that holds `subds` records only (Fusion Form, `TSplines.BlobParts`); the cage is the form's definition, not a state. The form's B-rep evaluation is the state after the feature, with the limit-surface carriers. A Fusion form's cages are T-spline cages (`SubdScheme::TSpline`, §5.6). `SubdScheme::TSpline` states the rule set a cage declares in its `.tsm` header: `star-knot-rule NURCCS`, `star-smoothness 0`, `cap-type G1CAPS`, and `degree 3`. A Fusion writer writes those values, and a header value other than them is a value no decoder has met (part 11). `end-conditions` states how a cage encodes its sharp edges, which its crease edges and knot intervals state: `SUBD_CREASES` as a crease edge list and `MULTIPLE_KNOTS` as zero knot intervals. Which of the two a cage stores follows the engine that wrote it (`MULTIPLE_KNOTS` from engines 4.1.0 and earlier, `SUBD_CREASES` from 4.2.6 and later), so it is layout (Rule N case (b)), except at a boundary: there it stays the native option `f3d:end-conditions` (Rule N case (a), part 11). Edit selections and editor state stay native (Rule N case (b)). A SubD object (Rhino) is geometry: a body whose shell holds its cage (§5.6). A form states every cage it owns. Where the decoder does not establish the whole set, because it has not read the join between the form and its cage entries, because the stored evidence leaves the set open, or because a cage's entry is a given-up part (§3.3), the form is `Unresolved { family: Form }` (§6): a set the decoder assumes, or a part of the set, is not stated as `cage` (typed, carrier unread; part 11). The form's stored result remains its evaluation (§5.4). The source's references from the form to its cages (Fusion archive entries, serializer links, asset and type identifiers) are its encoding of `cage` and stay in its native record (§3.1).

- A `SheetMetalRule` is a record of the scope that holds sheet-metal defaults which several features and bodies share (D53): the Fusion rule record (a record of type `B42ED662-…`), the CATIA sheet-metal parameters, a SolidWorks Sheet-Metal feature's values. It is no member of a container. `ApplyRule` is a member that makes `rule` govern the bodies `bodies` selects, or the state's sheet-metal bodies where `bodies` is `None`, from its position on (CATIA sheet-metal parameters, a SolidWorks per-body Sheet-Metal feature, Fusion Change Sheet Metal Rule). A wall or flange names its rule where the source does (Fusion), and a wall's rule governs the body it makes. A sheet-metal feature field that is `None` takes the governing rule's value, and the target default where no rule governs (§2.4), except a `radius_side`, which no writer defaults (below). `ReliefShape::Rule` is the explicit choice of the rule's relief, and `Obround` a slot with half-round ends; a relief's width is `width`, or `width_ratio` times the thickness. `allowance` states how the flat length of a governed bend is found: `KFactor` by one K-factor, `KFactorTable` by a table of K-factors, `Table` by a bend table, and `Equations` by expressions of the bend's own angle, radius, and thickness. `KFactorTable` is a bend table that states the K-factor by the ratio of a bend's inside radius to the thickness: its rows, in increasing ratio, each map a ratio to a K-factor. `lookup` states how a bend takes its K-factor from them: `NextAtOrAbove` the K-factor of the first row whose ratio is not below the bend's own; `Linear` the linear interpolation between the two rows whose ratios bracket it. Under either, a bend whose ratio lies above every row takes the last row's K-factor, and one below every row the first row's. The FreeCAD SheetMetal add-on reads its table from a spreadsheet with a `Radius / Thickness` column and a `K-factor (ANSI)` or `K-factor (DIN)` column; its unfolder at `v0.2.60-beta` and the legacy unfolder on its master branch look up `NextAtOrAbove`, and the new unfolder on master interpolates (`lookup.py` and `SheetMetalUnfolder.py` at `v0.2.60-beta`, `SheetMetalNewUnfolder.py` at `c505f5ea`). The new unfolder's segment search picks the first segment for any ratio inside a table of three or more rows, so it extrapolates that segment: a defect of that producer, not a law (part 11). A decoder states `lookup` only where the file records which unfolder produced it; no FreeCAD file does, so the FreeCAD decoder states `None`. Its K-factors are in the ANSI convention, the neutral axis's distance from the inside face over the thickness, so the decoder halves a DIN value, as the add-on does. A writer whose target takes one K-factor writes the K-factor for the governed bends' ratio and charges a loss naming the rule; one whose target's table law differs from `lookup`, or where `lookup` is `None` and the two laws give different K-factors for a governed bend, charges a loss naming the rule. `Table` states a bend's flat length by its thickness, inside radius, and angle: one block per thickness, each a column of radii, a column of angles, and a value per angle and radius, `values[i][j]` for `angles[i]` and `radii[j]`. `angle` states what the angle column is: `Deflection`, the rotation of the bent flange from the unbent wall, or `Opening`, 180° less it; `None` is not read. `value` states what a cell is. An `Allowance` is the length of the bend's neutral arc, in the document's length unit, which the flat pattern adds to the flanges measured to the bend's tangent lines. A `Deduction` is the length x, in that unit, by which the flat length falls short of the two flange lengths, L = A + B − x, and `flanges` states where A and B run to: `OuterSharp`, the intersection of the two outer faces, at every deflection; `OuterSharpThenTangent`, that intersection up to a deflection of 90° and above it, for each flange, the plane tangent to the bend's outer face and perpendicular to that flange, a setback of the inside radius plus the thickness; `None` states neither, so the deduction is defined up to 90° of deflection, where the two agree, and is not established above it. A `KFactor` cell is the K-factor the bend takes. `lookup` states, for each of the table's three axes, how a bend is read whose thickness, inside radius, or angle is not an entry of that axis: `Exact`, the bend takes the entry equal to its own value, within the source's tolerance, and a bend with no such entry lies outside the grid; `Linear`, the cell varies linearly between the two entries that bracket the bend's value, along each such axis where more than one is `Linear`; `None`, the law of that axis is not stated. `outside` states what a bend outside the grid takes: `BackupKFactor`, the K-factor in its `k_factor`, which is `None` where the source's carrier of it is not read; an `outside` of `None` does not state it. SolidWorks stores a bend table that a part uses whole (`uoBendTable_c` in `Contents/Definition`: the quantity's name, then one `uoGaugeBendTableSection_c` per thickness with its angles, its radii, and its cells, angle by radius); where its quantity is "Bend Allowance", the SolidWorks decoder states it as `Table` with `value: Allowance` (part 11). A byte after the Sheet-Metal feature's table path selects the method: 1 the K-factor `D2`, which is `KFactor`; 4 the stored table; 2 a constant bend allowance; and 3 a constant bend deduction. The constant is the Sheet-Metal feature's `D3`, so the decoder states method 2 as `Equations` whose `BendEquations` has `yields: Allowance` and `angle: Deflection`, and method 3 the same with `yields: Deduction { flanges: None }`, each with one range from 0° to 180°, both bounds inclusive, whose value is `D3`. A part that uses no table stores the path of a table it does not read, an installed sample or a user's file, and empty axes, which is no table: the path stays a native option. Whether a SolidWorks table's angle column is the deflection or the opening angle is not read (`angle: None`). SolidWorks' page says that the software "interpolates" where the part's thickness or the bend's angle falls between the table's values, and names neither the law nor the radius (Bend Table Overview); that constructs no result, so the SolidWorks decoder states no axis of `lookup` and no `outside`. A deduction or K-factor table, which that page defines ("You must measure the bend deduction (BD) from the virtual sharp"), is held by no stored file known to the project; a SolidWorks deduction table is `Deduction { flanges: None }`, since the page does not say where the flanges run above 90° of deflection (typed from the page, carrier unread; part 11). The gauge table the part stores beside its bend table (`uoSMEnvironmentTable_c`) offers thicknesses and radii for the part to choose from and decides no geometry once they are chosen, so it is the source setting `sldprt:gauge_table` (Rule N case (b)). Inventor stores its bend table inside the part: a rule of method 2 references one record of type `19923810` per thickness, holding the thickness, an opening-angle column, a radius column, and the grid, and closing with three f64. Its `angle` is `Opening`, which Autodesk's page states. Its `value` is `Deduction { flanges: Some(OuterSharpThenTangent) }`, read from Inventor's own stored unfolding of bends under a table rule, whose bend-extent edges give each bend zone's flat width (part 11). Its `lookup` states `angle: Linear`, and, from Autodesk's pages, `radius: Linear` ("determined by linear interpolation"), `thickness: Exact` (a block serves its own thickness within a "Tolerance (+/-) for sheet thickness"), and `outside: BackupKFactor` ("Backup KFactor Value: value passed to the internal solver if a request falls outside of the defined bend table") (About Bend Tables, To Work with Bend Tables). Each rule stores two equal K-factor expressions and no stored file known to the project settles which is the backup, so the decoder states `BackupKFactor { k_factor: None }` (typed, carrier unread; part 11). The three f64 that close a block are read as its end tolerances (inferred from their count and the page's default) and stay native options, and a cell of 0 is stored as written. `Equations` states the allowance as expressions: `ranges` divide the bend's angle, measured as `angle` states, into intervals in increasing order, each including or excluding its `from` and its `to` as its two flags state, and a bend whose angle lies in a range takes that range's `value`, an expression of the bend's own angle, inside radius, and thickness (the `Bend` variables of §5.13). `yields` states what the value is: `Allowance`, `Deduction`, and `KFactor` as a table's cell is, and `Compensation`, a length v that the flat length adds to the two flange lengths, L = A + B + v, with A and B measured as `flanges` states. A compensation is a deduction of the opposite sign; it is an arm of its own because the expression is the author's text, which negating it would rewrite. `Native` keeps a quantity whose stored code is not read. Inventor's equation rule (unfold method 4) is `Equations`. Its `kind` is 1 `Compensation` and 4 `KFactor`, read from what the stored expressions compute: under `kind` 1, a length that subtracts the two flange setbacks; under `kind` 4, a number divided by the thickness. `kind` 2 and 3, which no stored file known to the project holds on an equation rule, are `Native("inventor:bend_equation:<kind>")` (part 11). Its `ref` is 3 `Opening` and 2 `Deflection` (inferred from the stored expressions; Autodesk's page names the two references). Each range record (`fd803147`) holds a lower and an upper bound, the variable's name, two flags, and the expression; the flags are read as the bounds' inclusion (inferred: so read, the stored ranges cover the angles with no overlap). The expressions name three variables and no other, β the angle, ρ the inside radius, and μ the thickness, which are `Bend(Angle)`, `Bend(InsideRadius)`, and `Bend(Thickness)`. Where a rule computes DIN 6935's compensation term for term, subtracting 2(ρ + μ) for opening angles up to 90° and 2(ρ + μ)·tan of half the deflection from 90° to 165°, it subtracts the two setbacks, at the same angle, of Inventor's unfolding of a table bend. So the decoder states `Compensation { flanges: Some(OuterSharpThenTangent) }` for a rule with those ranges, which is inferred from the expressions, and `flanges: None` for any other rule (part 11). The rule's three f64 stay native options. A SolidWorks bend calculation table (`sldprt:bend_calculation_table`), which no stored file known to the project holds, and NX's bend allowance and bend deduction formula texts (`nx:bend_allowance_formula`, `nx:bend_deduction_formula`), a template default that a stored flat does not follow, stay native options of the rule (Rule N case (a), part 11). CATIA stores no bend table: the part-level `BendTable` is the empty default. Its K-factor is `KFactor` bound to a parameter whose expression is the stored `DINNormaFormula`, which equals K = ½ − ¼·log10(min(100, max(5t/r, 1))) for thickness t and inside radius r; which quantity the formula's second argument binds is inferred (part 11). An NX sheet-metal part states `KFactor` bound to its neutral-factor expression (`Sheet_Metal_Neutral_Factor`; part 11). Its table name is a string with no rows behind it. A Creo part states `KFactor` 2y/π from its `def_y_factor` y: the developed lengths its walls and bends store follow (π/2·r + y·t)·θ/90°. A Creo part that uses a bend table stores only the table's name, and its bends do not follow its Y-factor, so the Creo decoder states `allowance: None` for a part that names a table. A bend table that a source names and does not store (Creo, NX, a SolidWorks path) is not content of the file: the name stays the native option `<codec>:bend_table` of the rule (Rule N case (a): the table's rows are in no stored file known to the project), and a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the rule. A `Table` whose `angle` is `None`, or whose `Deduction` states no `flanges`, is written back unchanged by a writer of the source's own format; any other target writes its default and charges a loss naming the rule, since it cannot say what a cell gives every governed bend. A writer whose target has bend tables writes any other `Table` as its own table, restating the angle column and the quantity where its own differ, which each cell's thickness, radius, and angle allow, and charges a loss naming the rule where its lookup differs from `lookup` or an axis of `lookup` is `None`. A writer whose target takes no bend table writes, for such a `Table`, the K-factor each governed bend's cell gives, and charges a loss naming the rule. A writer whose target has no equation rule writes for `Equations` the K-factor each governed bend's range gives and charges a loss naming the rule; where `yields` is `Native`, or a `Compensation` or `Deduction` states no `flanges` and a governed bend deflects more than 90°, it writes its default and charges the loss. Fusion stores no table, and no rule references a table record. The Fusion decoder reads a rule's one K-factor as the f64 after the LP-UTF16 GUID that follows the rule's four-times-thickness member, the scalar that opens the rule's material trailer; that reading is an assumption no stored file sets against a flat length, so the decoder states `allowance: None` and keeps the value as the native option `f3d:rule_k_factor` (Rule N case (a), part 11). The SolidWorks Sheet-Metal Master node, an anonymous sentinel with no parameters that parts without sheet metal also hold, emits nothing.
- `Wall` makes a flat sheet from a closed profile (Fusion base flange, Inventor face and plate, CATIA wall, a SolidWorks base flange on a closed profile, a Creo wall that is neither attached nor a contour). `NormalSide` places the thickness relative to the profile's oriented normal. A SolidWorks base flange (`moSMBaseFlange_c`) frames its profile reference, and the record's shape says whether the profile is closed (inferred from the shape): a record with one child and no depth of its own is a closed plate and is `Wall`, its thickness the Sheet-Metal feature's `D7`; one with base-bend children is open and is `ContourFlange` (below); and one with one child and a depth of its own is not separated and stays `Native("sldprt:base_flange")` until its sketch is read. Where the profile is a later sketch whose reference is not numbered, a decoder resolves it to one of these kinds (part 11). `Flange` grows a wall from sheet edges (Fusion edge flange, Inventor flange). `angle` is the bend's sweep, the angle the wall turns through from the plane of the face the edge bounds, in every format. `PerEdge` holds one pair per selected edge, in edge order. `CenteredPerEdge` centres each edge's flange on that edge's midpoint with a width of its own, one width per selected edge in edge order (a Fusion edge flange whose widths are per edge stores one symmetric width per edge, in the order of its edge groups). A Fusion edge flange whose width is bounded at each edge by two boundary groups and two signed offsets keeps them as native options with `width: None`: which offset belongs to which boundary, and which end each boundary bounds, are not read (Rule N case (a), part 11). A Fusion flange whose width the decoder does not read, a reference-framed width record whose offset pair it does not decode included, states `width: None` with the values it reads as native options (typed, carrier unread; part 11). A Fusion flange whose stored bend radius is 0 is `SheetMetalKind::Native` with its kind and the radius as a native option: a `BendSpec.radius` is positive, and no stored file known to the project shows the bend a radius of 0 builds (Rule N case (a), part 11). `height_datum` states the line a flange's `Distance` height is measured from: `InnerSharp` the intersection of the base's and the flange's inner faces, `OuterSharp` that of their outer faces, and `TangentToBend` the line tangent to the bend and parallel to the flange. `position` states where the bend lies against the selected edge: `MaterialInside` puts the reference plane through the base's other edge with the flange's material inside it, so the bend starts inside the outer edges; `MaterialOutside` puts it through the selected edge with the material outside; `AtEdge` makes the side face the reference plane, with the bend starting at the selected edge; and `TangentToSide` makes the side face the reference plane, with the bend tangent to it where the angle is 90° or more (Fusion Flange reference and API `FlangeHeightDatumTypes` and `BendPositionTypes`). `height_datum` decides how a `Distance` height is read, so where it is `None` a writer of another codec does not write the height and charges a loss naming the feature (§2.4). `outline` is the wall's outline, an open chain sketched in the wall's own plane: the sketch plane is the wall's face on the side `height_datum` names (`InnerSharp` the inner face, `OuterSharp` the outer), the chain's two free ends lie on that sharp, and the wall's material runs from that face across the thickness; the outline gives the wall's height and width, and its sketch plane with the face the edge bounds gives the bend's sweep, so a `Flange` with an `outline` states none of the three, on its one edge. Fusion stores the datum as the API value plus one, 1 `InnerSharp` and 2 `OuterSharp` (part 11), and `TangentToBend` is 3 by the same offset. It stores the position as the API value, 1 `MaterialOutside`, 2 `MaterialInside`, 3 `AtEdge`, and 4 `TangentToSide`. Fusion's `Legacy` position, stored 0, stays the native option `f3d:bend_position`: no stored file known to the project holds it (Rule N case (a), part 11). A writer whose target lacks the datum or the position charges a loss naming the feature.
- `Bend` bends existing sheet metal along `line`, a sketch line or an edge, by `angle` with the bend `radius` (Creo bend, feature type 953; Inventor Fold, whose `FoldDefinition` holds a bend line, an angle, and a radius). A rolled bend states `flat_length`, the length of flat sheet it rolls at `radius`, in place of `angle` (Creo: a rolled bend "is defined by both the radius and the amount of flat material to bend", PTC About Bending Walls). A field that is `None` takes the governing rule's value (D53). `angle` is the bend's deflection, the rotation of the bent flange from the unbent wall: a Creo bend whose angle dimension is 120 turns its flange's outer face by 120°, an included angle of 60° (part 11). `radius_side` states which radius `radius` is, here and in a `BendSpec`: `Inside` the inner bend radius, `Outside` the inner radius plus the thickness; `None` is not stated, and no writer defaults it (§2.4): a writer of another codec does not take its target's side, and writes the feature's stored result (§3.4, lowering step 3) or charges a loss naming the feature; a writer of the same codec re-emits the source form. A source whose bend radius has one fixed side states that side. Creo stores both, inner and outer radius dimensions; no stored instruction separates them, so the Creo decoder reads the side from the cylinder whose radius equals the dimension. `zone` places the bend's developed zone, whose length is the bend's developed length under the governing allowance (θ(r + k·t) for its deflection θ in radians, inside radius r, thickness t, and K-factor k where a K-factor governs), against `line`: `MovingSide` wholly on the side that moves, starting at the line, so the fixed flat ends at the line; `FixedSide` wholly on the fixed side, ending at the line, so the fixed flat ends that length short of it; `Centered` centred on it, so the fixed flat ends half that length short of it. `line_face` states which face of the bent sheet the line lies on: `Inner`, the moving flange turning toward the side the line's face faces, or `Outer`. `fixed_side` states which side of the line stays put: `Left` the side of d × m, d the line's direction and m the outward normal of the sheet face that carries the line, and `Right` the other. A `MovingSide` or `FixedSide` zone whose `fixed_side` is `None` cannot be placed, and a `line_face` of `None` leaves the way the flange turns unstated: for either a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the feature. Creo stores the zone in the bend section's `order_ptr.flip`, bit 64 `MovingSide`, 128 `FixedSide`, and 256 `Centered`. Creo stores `fixed_side` and `line_face` against the section's z, n, and the line's direction d from its `end1` to its `end2`: `order_ptr.flip` bit 32, equal to the section's `attributes` bit 1024, puts the fixed side on d × n where set and on n × d where clear, and the sign of placement instruction 403's offset, the signed angle, turns the moving side toward −n where positive and toward +n where negative. The design states both against m, the outward normal of the face that carries the line, so the decoder finds from the stored faces whether the section faces out of the sheet, n = m, or into it, n = −m, and states bit 32 set as `Left` and a positive angle as `Outer` where n = m, swapping both where n = −m; no stored field of the bend states which (the sketch plane row's `orient` and the section's `plane_flip` and `flip` are 1 on every bend). A rolled bend stores no angle; a roll turns toward −n, under Rule H1: the decoder states `line_face` for a roll only where the stored cylinders agree, and `None` otherwise (part 11). The Inventor Fold stores the three in its property list: slot 0, 0 `Centered`, 1 `MovingSide`, and 2 `FixedSide`; slot 1, 1 `Inner` and 0 `Outer`; slot 2, 0 `Left` and 1 `Right`. The `FixedSide` reading is thin (part 11). A writer whose target lacks one of the three charges a loss naming the feature. A bend option whose meaning is not established is a native option of the feature, keyed by its format's own name (`creo:<code>`, `inventor:<name>`, §6; Rule N case (a), part 11). A Fusion bend stores its lines and one angle per line. Where it has one line and its stored angle is positive, `angle` binds that angle's parameter. Which line each angle of a bend of several lines belongs to is not read, and what a negative stored angle bends is not established, so such a bend states `angle: None` and keeps its angles as the native option `f3d:bend_angle` (Rule N case (a), part 11). The face it keeps stationary is read on an assumption, so it states `fixed_side: None` and keeps that face as the native option `f3d:bend_stationary` (Rule N case (a), part 11).
- `Connect` joins sheet faces with a bend, which `between` names. `Apart` joins two sheet faces that do not touch: it picks one model edge on each face, the bend has the governing rule's radius and thickness unless `radius` states one, and the faces are extended to the bend (`AlignedToSideFaces`) or met by a section perpendicular to them (`PerpendicularToSideFaces`) (Inventor Bend: "Bend features can join sheet metal faces that do not touch", To Work with Bend Features help and API `BendDefinition.ExtendFaces`). `double` states a connect between two parallel faces that are not coplanar. `EqualBends` joins the two edges where they lie by two equal bends, tangent to each other or with a flat between, trimming or extending neither face. `Deg45` and `Deg90` keep the edge `fixed` names, trim or extend the other face, and join them by two bends of 45° or 90°, with a flat between the two where they are not tangent. `FullRadius` keeps the edge `fixed` names, trims or extends the other face, and joins them by one bend of 180°, each of whose radii is half the distance between the two faces it is tangent to, so `radius` plays no part. `First` and `Second` name the members of `Apart`; `fixed: None` does not state which is kept. Inventor's double bend is so (Autodesk's Bends Dialog Reference). An Inventor Bend at the top of the history, with an edge collection of its own, is a `Connect`: its option record holds two enumerations, (1, 1) on a single bend, which makes one cylinder pair of radii r and r + t, and on a double bend (3, 4) `EqualBends`, (6, 7) `Deg90`, and (6, 8) `FullRadius` (part 11). `Deg45` is held by no stored file known to the project and is typed from the page, and `Deg90` is read from its flat's angle, which equal bends give only where the two edges lie exactly opposite. The page states both edges as the default fixed one, and the stored flag is not read, so the decoder states `fixed: None` (typed, carrier unread; part 11). `SharedEdge` picks one edge that two sheet faces of one body already share, and replaces the corner the two faces make there by a bend tangent to both, of inner radius `radius` and outer radius `radius` plus the thickness, its axis parallel to the edge in the plane that bisects the corner. An Inventor top-level Bend of option pair (2, 1), which stores one edge in slot 0 and its radius in slot 1, is so. The arm falls under Rule H1: the Inventor decoder states `ConnectBetween::SharedEdge` only where the stored bend's faces replace the corner so (two coaxial cylinders of radii `radius` and `radius` plus the thickness, tangent to both faces on the edge, their axis parallel to it), and `SheetMetalKind::Native("inventor:bend")` with its edge, radius, and option pair kept otherwise. The record also names one of the two faces on the edge, which adds nothing a reader needs and is not carried; the first enumeration's value 2 is the shared-edge form, against 1 for two faces that do not touch. Any other pair of values on a top-level Bend stays the native option `inventor:bend_option` (Rule N case (a), part 11). The same record and enumerations sit on the Bend records that flanges, faces, and contour flanges own (where the second value 4 occurs on bends with no double form), so the decoder reads `double` from them only on a top-level Bend. An Inventor Bend record that a Flange, Contour Flange, or Face references is that feature's bend, neither a `Bend` nor a `Connect`: a flange's bend is its `Flange.bend`, with the bend record's radius and the relief its plate shares. A Face's bend whose edge collection names the Face's own plate makes the bend between the new wall and the sheet it meets, and the file names that sheet's face by no pick, so its radius and relief stay native options of the `Wall` (`inventor:face_bend`), for which a writer of another codec charges a loss naming the feature; one with an empty edge collection makes no face and is no option. A writer whose target has no such bend, or lacks the `double` form, charges a loss naming the feature.
- `Rip` cuts sheet metal without bending it. `Faces` removes the wall under each picked face, and the walls that meet it stay whole up to the face's surface. `Along` cuts the sheet through its thickness along `path`, its two walls normal to the sheet where they stand, and `width` states what the cut removes: `Tear` nothing, the two lips coinciding, and `Gap` the lips `gap` apart, placed by `side` (`None`: not stated). `RipPath::Ruling` runs from `at`, a point on the boundary of `face`, along the straight line in `face` to the point at the same fraction of the opposite boundary edge: the ruling of a cylinder or cone, or a corner's side edge. `Line` runs straight in `face` between two points on its boundary. `Edges` runs along each picked edge where two walls meet and cuts both walls back from it, set back from the solid's edge as `Convert` states (below); it occurs only in a `ConvertRip` (part 10), since no stored file known to the project holds a rip feature outside a conversion with a built body (the SolidWorks Rip feature is `Native`, below). An `Edges` path lies in two faces and has no direction, so it has no `Left` or `Right` side. `Sketched` runs along each curve of the sketched chain, as `through` states: `SketchWall` cuts the one wall the sketch lies on, along the chain; `Projected` carries the chain along its sketch's normal until it meets the sheet and splits the sheet there through its thickness, normal to the sheet, with zero width. `KerfSide` places the gap against a `Ruling`, `Line`, or `Sketched` path, d being the path's direction and m the outward normal of the face it lies in: `Centered` puts the path midway between the lips, and `Left` and `Right` put one lip through the path and the gap on the side of d × m or m × d, the sides `LineSide` names. How decoders state each arm:
  - `Faces`: a Creo surface rip cuts out the picked wall, and its neighbours end on its plane, not one thickness back (that the wall's inner face goes with it is inferred). PTC's About Ripping Material says the same ("Surface Rip—Cuts out an entire surface patch from the model and removes volume"), as do Autodesk's Fusion Rip reference ("Select a sheet metal face to remove") and Inventor's To Rip page ("A Face Extents rip removes any entire selected face"). The Creo decoder states `Faces` under Rule H1: only where the stored faces show the picked wall cut out and its neighbours ending on its plane, and `Native("creo:1006")` with its picks kept otherwise. No stored file known to the project holds a Fusion or Inventor face rip, so both stay `SheetMetalKind::Native` with their picks until a file holds one.
  - `Ruling`: Inventor single-point rips. From an edge's midpoint on a planar face the cut leaves at a right angle and meets the opposite edge at its midpoint; from a corner of a planar face it runs along the face's side edge from that corner to the base's corner; and from a point on the rim of a cylinder or right cone it is the ruling through the point; between these points the rule is inferred. The arm is under Rule H1: the decoder states it only where the stored walls give that cut, and `Native` otherwise. `Line`: Inventor's point-to-point rip, the cut the straight line between its two points; under Rule H1 likewise.
  - `Edges` with `Gap`: SolidWorks convert rips on edges, which are `ConvertRip`s: where the sheet lies outside the solid's faces (`Outside`), both walls stand `T cot(t/2) + gap / (2 sin(t/2))` back from the solid's edge, the walls' inner edges `gap + 2 T cos(t/2)` apart; where the sheet lies `Inside` and the solid's edge is the line where the walls' outer planes meet, the walls' inner edges lie `gap` apart (inferred) (`Convert`, below).
